#4240. Arc Raiders just keeps breaking its own Steam player records

Word of mouth has done wonders for the popularity of Arc Raiders, clearly more than all the pre-launch marketing and hype.

Arc Raiders just cannot be stopped. The extraction shooter from Embark Studios has once again attracted more players over the weekend than it has in its launch week, and over its first weekend on the market.

The positive reception the PvPvE game has garnered from players has clearly caused many of them to convince their friends to jump into this unique gem of a game.

The day Arc Raiders launched, it peaked at 264,673 concurrent players on Steam. Although not massive, it was quite a bit more than the game’s most popular - free - beta test managed to attract.

That figure was broken yet again over the game’s first weekend, with Arc Raiders having reached 354,836 concurrent players on Steam. This is where many thought it would settle, as we start to see the gradual - and expected - decline of player numbers.

To everyone’s surprise, however, Arc Raiders shattered even that record yet again on Sunday, November 9. According to SteamDB, the game peaked at 462,488 concurrent players on Steam, which is a sizeable increase on its launch day numbers. Indeed, should this trend continue, Arc Raiders is going to be well on its way to doubling its initial launch record.

While a few games have broken their launch Steam player records in the past, it’s incredibly rare to see it happen - especially twice in such a short period after launch. Embark clearly has a winner on its hands here.

Arc Raiders’ next big moment is the game’s first post-launch map, which is set to arrive at some point this month, alongside new Quests and other gameplay items. Seeing as how the Steam concurrent record has been broken twice, there’s every chance the arrival of the new map will bring another boost to player numbers.

If you’re among the millions of players who have been exploring the Rust Belt, you’re probably wondering where to find prickly pears, where to find lemons and apricots, and where to find olives - and those links will answer all of those questions. And, if you just jumped in over the weekend, you’re definitely going to find these Arc Raiders tips very helpful.

#4239. T1 beat Karmine Corp 3-1 to reach sixth straight Worlds semi-final against Bilibili Gaming

T1 are through to the Worlds 2026 semi-finals after ending Karmine Corp's run in four games. Bilibili Gaming now stand between the Korean side and a place in the Brooklyn final.

The quarter-final was played on Friday 6 November at the Credit Union of Texas Event Center in Allen, Texas. The Korean side took the first two games in 36 and 30 minutes. Karmine Corp pulled one back over 37 minutes. T1 then closed out the series in 35 minutes.

The result puts T1 in the Worlds semi-finals for a sixth year running, a streak that began in 2021, Sports Kyunghyang reported. Bilibili Gaming await them on Sunday 8 November, with a place in the final at stake.

Karmine Corp’s tournament began on 15 October. They beat Cloud9 3-2 in the Play-In. In the Swiss Stage, the French organisation opened with a 1-0 win over Anyone’s Legend. Defeats to LYON and Bilibili Gaming followed. Karmine Corp then beat CTBC Flying Oyster 2-0 and Movistar KOI 2-0 to reach the knockouts.

Karmine Corp sat 13th on 1785 in the Elo power rankings, just behind their opponents. The teams had also split their two earlier meetings this year. T1 won 3-0 at the Mid-Season Invitational on 29 June. Karmine Corp won 2-1 at the Esports World Cup on 18 July.

T1 reached the knockouts with wins over LOS, CTBC Flying Oyster and Movistar KOI. Their one Swiss Stage defeat came against Dplus KIA. Bilibili Gaming swept that same Dplus KIA side 3-0 in the first quarter-final on 5 November. In the Swiss Stage, they also beat Hanwha Life Esports 2-0 and Karmine Corp 1-0.

The most recent meeting between the semi-finalists went to Bilibili Gaming. That was a best-of-one in the Esports World Cup 2026 group stage.

The other semi-final is Gen.G against Invictus Gaming on Saturday 7 November at 16:00 Central Time. Gen.G beat LYON 3-0 in their quarter-final. Invictus Gaming beat Top Esports 3-1. Nineteen teams started the tournament, which has a total prize pool of $5,000,000.

#4238. AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death

More than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year. This deadly emergency occurs when the heart's electrical system suddenly fails, causing the heart to stop pumping blood. It can strike older adults with known heart conditions as well as seemingly healthy young athletes. Although implanted defibrillators can prevent some of these deaths, doctors have long struggled to determine which patients need them most.

Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.

The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden. By comparing the electrical patterns recorded in these scans with information from death certificates, the researchers taught an AI system to recognize subtle differences between healthy individuals, patients with known heart risks, and people who eventually died from sudden cardiac causes.

The team then evaluated the technology using thousands of additional patient records from the United States and Taiwan, testing whether the patterns could reliably identify people at heightened risk in different populations.

AI Detects Hidden Heart Risks That Standard Tests Miss

The results suggest that AI can identify vulnerable patients more effectively than the conventional tests doctors typically rely on. Current screening methods largely focus on how much blood the heart pumps with each contraction, a measurement used to assess whether someone might benefit from an implanted defibrillator.

Using these traditional measurements, doctors can identify a group of patients with an annual sudden cardiac death rate of 4.6%. The AI system, however, identified a group with an annual death rate of 7%, demonstrating a greater ability to distinguish patients facing serious danger.

Importantly, the algorithm also recognized a broader population of people at elevated risk, including thousands who would not normally raise concerns under existing medical guidelines. Most of these individuals would have been classified as relatively low risk using conventional methods.

Another major advantage is that the AI system works with ordinary EKG images, which are already routinely collected in hospitals and medical centers around the world. This means the technology could potentially improve screening without requiring an entirely new type of medical test.

The findings, published in Nature, could eventually help physicians make more informed decisions about who should receive an implanted defibrillator. They also raise an intriguing scientific question about what changes inside the heart produce the electrical patterns that AI has learned to recognize.

"Medical decisions are really hard, and I think that's why AI is so exciting for me," said Ziad Obermeyer, an associate professor at UC Berkeley's School of Public Health and the study's lead author. "We can not only make better decisions, but also start to understand what's actually going on with these patients before their heart stops."

Why Sudden Cardiac Death Is So Difficult to Predict

Sudden cardiac arrest is different from a heart attack. A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of the heart becomes blocked or severely restricted. Cardiac arrest, by contrast, results from a failure of the electrical signals that coordinate the heartbeat.

Immediate CPR and an electrical shock from an automated external defibrillator can sometimes restore the heart's rhythm. However, roughly 90% of people who experience sudden cardiac arrest outside a hospital die within minutes, making early recognition of those at risk especially important.

For Obermeyer, an emergency physician whose research combines artificial intelligence, medicine, and health policy, sudden cardiac death remains one of medicine's most frustrating unsolved problems.

Because victims often die without warning, researchers have limited opportunities to observe what happens inside the heart immediately before it stops. An autopsy may uncover blocked blood vessels, hardened tissue, or other structural abnormalities, but it cannot fully reveal how the heart was functioning in the moments leading up to death.

"One thing that makes the problem very tragic, but also very well suited for AI, is that we have the cure for this problem," Obermeyer said. "If you knew you were one of the people who was going to drop dead, you would go to a cardiologist and you'd get a defibrillator implanted. The problem is that doctors can't figure out who needs one before it's too late."

The Problem With Current Heart Risk Screening

Doctors currently rely heavily on a measurement of how effectively the heart pushes blood out with each beat. Patients whose hearts pump below a specified threshold may be considered candidates for an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, a device that can deliver an electrical shock when a dangerous heart rhythm develops.

But obtaining this measurement generally requires a more extensive medical evaluation. Many people who eventually experience sudden cardiac arrest never receive such testing because they have no obvious reason to suspect they are in danger.

The approach also has limitations for patients who are identified as high risk. About two-thirds of implanted defibrillators in these patients never need to deliver a shock. As a result, many individuals undergo expensive, invasive procedures for potentially fatal emergencies that may never occur.

At the same time, thousands of people who are not recognized as being at risk die unexpectedly each year.

"In some fraction of those people, we could have prevented those deaths if we had just known it in time," Obermeyer said. "There are a lot of lives being lost from people who are dropping dead of sudden cardiac death that are preventable if we just had better AI tools to find these things."

The researchers hope that identifying more accurate warning signs could help doctors direct preventive treatments toward the patients most likely to benefit.

How Researchers Trained AI to Recognize Deadly Heart Patterns

Developing the algorithm required three independent collections of medical data gathered from different parts of the world.

The researchers began with six years of EKG recordings from Sweden's unified healthcare system. By linking these scans to death certificates, they could examine the electrical patterns of patients who later experienced sudden cardiac death and compare them with those of other patients.

The AI learned to identify combinations of spikes, waves, and other characteristics in the recordings that appeared to be associated with increased risk. Once the system had been trained, the team tested it against two additional datasets: two years of anonymized EKG records from a San Diego hospital system and a separate collection of patient data from Taipei.

This international testing helped researchers evaluate whether the algorithm's predictive abilities extended beyond the Swedish population used to develop it.

"Good AI starts with good data," said Obermeyer, who is also part of the joint UCSF-UC Berkeley Computational Precision Health program. "Unfortunately, data like the ones we used for this study are incredibly hard to access. It's a big part of why there's so little clinical AI in use today."

Obtaining and organizing the information was itself a massive undertaking. According to Obermeyer, assembling the datasets took approximately 10 years and involved contributions from two organizations he helped establish, Dandelion Health and Nightingale Open Science. Both organizations work to advance medical research through better access to data and artificial intelligence.

"It's one of the tremendous luxuries of being at Berkeley," Obermeyer said. "You can pursue these projects that just are a slow burn and then have -- hopefully -- a big return when they get over the finish line."

From Hidden Heart Signals to Lifesaving Treatments

The researchers have already begun exploring how the system might be used in actual healthcare settings.

Obermeyer is collaborating with medical systems in Sweden, Taiwan, and the United States to introduce the algorithm into hospital EKG databases. The goal is to examine existing heart scans for signs of elevated risk and identify patients who may benefit from additional monitoring.

Under the proposed approach, physicians would contact patients whose EKGs receive a high-risk assessment and offer them the opportunity to wear a patch that continuously records their heart's electrical activity.

These longer recordings could provide valuable clues about the biological processes responsible for the warning signals detected by the AI. Understanding those processes could help researchers explain why certain hearts are more vulnerable to suddenly developing fatal electrical disturbances.

For some patients, the additional information might ultimately support a recommendation to receive an implanted defibrillator, potentially preventing a sudden and otherwise unexpected death.

Obermeyer has also created a website where people interested in learning about their own risk can provide basic personal information and an email address. The research team can then contact them about EKG analysis when the technology becomes more widely available.

Could AI Reveal New Secrets About the Human Heart?

Beyond its potential to improve the prevention of sudden cardiac death, the discovery highlights how artificial intelligence could help scientists investigate medical mysteries that have resisted conventional approaches.

Rather than simply identifying patients who might need treatment, the algorithm has uncovered patterns in heart activity that researchers do not yet fully understand. Studying those signals could lead to new insights into the electrical disturbances responsible for sudden cardiac death and potentially reveal additional opportunities for prevention.

Obermeyer believes this ability to uncover previously unrecognized biological patterns could become one of AI's most important contributions to medicine, opening new directions for research while helping physicians make better decisions.

"There is also going to be a new way of doing science that comes out of these tools," Obermeyer said, "and it's fun to think about how that starts happening."

Materials provided by University of California - Berkeley. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4237. Battlefield 6 patch finally ends the menace of the Lock-Guided Missile, shuts down the Recon Drone Sledgehammer exploit and more

Today's Battlefield 6 patch is laser-focused on taking care of some of the more infuriating bugs while also taking out a couple of exploits.

The next Battlefield 6 update is here. Having gone live just moments ago, update 1.1.1.5 is something of a midseason update, bringing a few quality of life tweaks to the game alongside some key fixes for a few of the issues that cropped up since the launch of Season 1 in late October.

This latest release is also the first to tackle some of the problems players have been running into playing Redsec battle royale, the free-to-play component that also came out recently.

Patch 1.1.1.5 is fairly limited in scope. The biggest fix in this one comes to the Lock-Guided Missiles going through flares, and generally being annoying enough to stop players from using air vehicles altogether.

The Lock-Guided Missiles were mainly used by AA vehicles, but they could also be equipped by IFVs, which made it even more of a nightmare to pilots. It got so bad that Battlefield Studios disabled it entirely while the team worked on a proper fix.

Another exploit the patch fixes is the one that allowed players to stand on the Recon Drone and reach areas they’re not supposed to. This was done by… repeatedly hitting it with a Sledgehammer. The long-running issue of vehicles not spawning for certain teams in Conquest and Breakthrough appears to have finally been fixed, too.

In terms of battle royale, the patch has a few fixes that should help make the experience more consistent, as well as improve the flow of matches. One of the more interesting addresses an issue that could eliminate the entire squad instead of reviving dead teammates when using a Mobile Spawn.

Patch 1.1.1.5 also has yet more adjustments to weapon dispersion (bloom). Some of the casses it addresses include transitioning from sprint to firing in ADS, and others where it apparently scaled with player movement speed.

#4236. A 19-year study reveals a troubling link between napping and death

A daily nap may seem like a harmless way to recharge, but new research suggests that certain napping habits could provide important clues about a person's health as they age. Scientists have found that taking longer or more frequent naps, particularly in the morning, is associated with an increased risk of death among older adults.

Researchers from Mass General Brigham and Rush University Medical Center examined the napping patterns of 1,338 older adults over a period of up to 19 years. Their findings, published in JAMA Network Open, suggest that monitoring daytime sleep could help identify underlying medical conditions or early signs of declining health.

"Excessive napping later in life has been linked to neurodegeneration, cardiovascular diseases and even greater morbidity, but many of those findings rely on self-reported napping habits and leave out metrics like when and how regular those naps are," said lead author Chenlu Gao, PhD, an investigator in the Department of Anesthesiology at Mass General Brigham and an affiliated research fellow in the Division of Sleep and Circadian Disorders in the Department of Medicine. "Our study is one of the first to show an association between objectively measured nap patterns and mortality and suggests there is immense clinical value in tracking napping patterns to catch health conditions early."

Why Scientists Are Studying Daytime Napping

Daytime naps are common among older adults, with estimates suggesting that 20% to 60% regularly nap. An occasional nap can help restore energy and improve alertness, but excessive daytime sleeping in later life has been associated with several health concerns.

Despite these connections, researchers still have an incomplete understanding of how specific napping behaviors relate to long-term health. Many earlier studies depended on participants remembering and reporting their own sleep habits, which may not provide an accurate picture. They also often overlooked important details, such as how long naps lasted, when they occurred, and how much napping patterns changed from one day to the next.

To obtain more reliable measurements, the research team analyzed information from the Rush Memory and Aging Project. Launched in 1997, this long-running study was designed primarily to investigate memory, thinking abilities, and neurological decline among older adults in northern Illinois, most of whom were white.

Starting in 2005, participants wore wrist activity monitors for 10 days to record their daily periods of rest and movement. Researchers used these measurements to identify daytime sleep and assess nap duration, frequency, timing, and daily variation.

Longer and More Frequent Naps Linked to Higher Mortality Risk

By 2025, researchers had assembled up to 19 years of follow-up information from 1,338 participants. They then examined whether napping habits measured during the initial assessment were associated with the likelihood of dying from any cause during the subsequent years.

The results revealed several notable patterns. Older adults who slept longer during the day or took naps more frequently had higher mortality rates. The timing of naps also appeared to matter.

Each additional hour spent napping per day was associated with approximately a 13% higher mortality risk. Taking one additional nap per day was linked to about a 7% increase in risk.

One of the most striking findings involved morning naps. Participants who napped in the morning had a 30% higher mortality risk compared with those who napped in the afternoon.

However, not every aspect of napping was associated with poorer outcomes. Researchers found no increased mortality risk linked to irregular napping schedules, suggesting that changes in nap timing or duration from day to day were not necessarily indicators of greater risk.

Could Napping Habits Reveal Hidden Health Problems?

The researchers emphasize that their findings do not mean daytime naps directly cause health problems or shorten lives. Instead, excessive napping may reflect medical conditions or changes in the body that have not yet been recognized.

"It is important to note that this is correlation, not causation. Excessive napping is likely indicating underlying disease, chronic conditions, sleep disturbances, or circadian dysregulation," said Gao. "Now that we know there is a strong correlation between napping patterns and mortality rates, we can make the case to implement wearable daytime nap assessments to predict health conditions and prevent further decline."

These findings raise the possibility that wearable activity trackers could eventually become useful tools for monitoring health in older adults. By identifying changes in daytime sleep habits, healthcare professionals might be able to recognize warning signs of underlying illness, disrupted sleep cycles, or neurological decline earlier.

Although further research is needed to determine how effectively napping patterns can predict specific medical conditions, the study suggests that something as ordinary as a daily nap could provide valuable information about a person's overall health.

Study Authorship, Disclosures, and Funding

Authorship: In addition to Gao and Li, the Mass General Brigham researchers involved in the study include Ruixue Cai, Xi Zheng, Arlen Gaba, Lei Gao, and Kun Hu. Other contributors include Lei Yu, Aron S. Buchman, and David A. Bennett.

Disclosures: Li received a financial gift from iFutureLab to support research and has received consulting payments for serving on the iFutureLab-HEKA Scientific Advisory Board as Chair of Cardiac Dynamics and Honorary Life-Time Co-Founder. Li also received an honorarium for delivering a lecture at Shandong University.

Hu has received consulting fees for serving on the iFutureLab-HEKA Scientific Advisory Board as Chair of Medical Biodynamics and Honorary Life-Time Co-Founder. Mass General Brigham reviewed and managed the interests of both Li and Hu under its conflict of interest policies. These interests are unrelated to the present research.

Funding: The research received support from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine Foundation (290-FP-22), the Alzheimer's Association Research Fellowship to Promote Diversity (AARFD-22-928372), and the National Institute on Aging (RF1AG064312; R01AG083799).

Gao C. received additional funding from the National Heart Lung and Blood Institute (5T32HL007901). Li received support from the BrightFocus Foundation (A2020886S) and startup funding from the Department of Anesthesia, Critical Care and Pain Medicine at Massachusetts General Hospital. Hu also received startup funding from the same department.

Gao L. received additional support from the Alzheimer's Association (AACSF-23-1148490), National Institute on Aging (R03AG087439), American Academy of Sleep Medicine (352-DS-24), and National Institute of General Medical Sciences (R35GM160254).

The Rush Memory and Aging Project was funded by the National Institutes of Health (R01AG056352 and R01AG017917).

#4235. 10 Best Warhammer 40k Survivors in Warhammer Survivors

Shane is a Contributor for DualShockers writing guides and other materials. He has a degree in Game Design and Criticism.

While a lot of survivor-like games offer you plenty of characters to play, Warhammer Survivors, Warhammer's take on Vampire Survivors, takes it to a new level. With more than 40 characters to play as between both universes, you’re pretty spoiled for choice.

Just because there are a ton of characters to play, though, doesn’t mean they’re all particularly good. Some are a bit tougher to get the hang of than others, and some just have terrible stats.

Warhammer Survivors is a brutal spin-off of Vampire Survivors, pitting heroes from Warhammer 40,000 and Age of Sigmar against endless hordes of enemies while maintaining the addictive gameplay loop.

This list will give you the ten best survivors to play as in the Warhammer 40k universe, since heroes are not transferable between universes. Each one has their ups and downs, but for the most part, you’ll find one you'll be well suited to.

Of all the characters available in this wild roguelike game, Sister Superior Amalia Novena is undoubtedly the easiest to use. She comes with a weapon that keeps enemies at bay and will mostly wipe out low-level enemies in the early stages.

While she does have an upper limit, her increase in range for the first 30 levels can be a major game changer. She’s a great starter character to get a better feel for levels and for quickly completing objectives, without tricky mechanics to learn.

The thing about the lovely Canoness Aurora Veritas is that she’ll basically burn through waves of enemies like they’re nothing. Better weapons and status effects really help, especially when coming across the bosses with loads of health.

The only real downside is she also has an upper limit and doesn’t scale indefinitely. Her boosted range is helpful, but towards the end of runs, she just doesn’t have enough juice to really do much.

The Chaplain is a pretty average character when things get started, and their weapon isn’t all that reliable, but they can scale well into later game levels. Once you’ve unlocked plenty of weapons, you’ll pretty much always be getting a few followers with every level up.

The extra Range he gets, combined with the automatically boosted Veterancy, makes him a great candidate for almost any run. If you aren’t very far in your journey, though, he’s likely to be less than helpful.

Max is the definition of a run-and-gun FPS player, as he brings a Combat Shotgun and some serious ability strength with him. Gaining Strength with every level could see him scale incredibly quickly in the right build, making him stronger than most.

The fact that his ability has no upper limit means you can combine him with the Gauntlet passive to potentially double your damage. This will let him tear through hordes of enemies without any concern for his safety.

In terms of weapons, Sergeant Furan isn’t exactly rocking the best one there is, but he definitely makes up for it in other areas. If you stay healthy, you’ll be earning a lot more Skill, and if you find yourself in trouble, taking some damage can let you wipe out a horde.

With no upper limit to his scaling, Furan can get pretty powerful, especially with the right build of weapons and passives. A bit difficult to use when starting, but it does give you more control over the buff you have currently.

Warhammer Survivors takes the familiar Vampire Survivors formula and adds a fresh twist: players must forge a weapon to fight boss monsters.

There’s nothing better than running your enemies over and hearing their bones crush beneath your treads, which is exactly what Knight-Commander Pask is all about. With bonuses to Strength, Save, and Toughness, he’s a machine of war.

Thanks to that limitless scaling, after just ten levels you’ll be gaining a lot of Wounds back every second to keep you in the fight. He’s also a giant tank, and who doesn’t love driving a massive tank through their enemies?

Saint Celestine might seem like an angelic being, but when it comes to killing, she’s a total demon and can get some absurd builds going. She’s got extra speed and just gets better with every level you manage to acquire.

She even starts with a bonus to Chance and two extra Redeployments, all things that will make a run much easier from the outset. You won’t have an easy time getting the hang of her, but when you do, she’s truly a beast. That movement speed is just valuable.

One of the hardest characters to use thanks to her starting weapon, Aveline still tops the charts when it comes to dealing with enemies. Her weapon is tough to use, but when combined with the bonuses she gets to Range and Move, she can become very powerful very quickly.

She also comes with built-in Corruption and a free Banish, which definitely helps her in terms of gaining levels and getting what she wants. With a smart build, she can effectively wipe out a massive line of enemies in one go.

Daedalosus is a Technoarchaeologist, and he’s bringing the weirdness to the game in more ways than one. His permanent ability to always have four choices at level-up automatically makes him one of the best in the game, since that helps you to round out a build faster. He's amazingly versatile.

While not exactly the most busted in terms of raw power, he can be a great way to get coins quickly, which is only further improved by his 30% bonus to Tithe. He’ll need a good setup to get going, but once he’s going, he’s hard to stop in this strange roguelike.

As the very last survivor to unlock in the 40k setting, High Abbess Morvenn Vahl is an absolute powerhouse by every standard. With boosts to virtually every single stat in the game, and the extra utility of gaining bonus stats for each Adepta Sororitas follower, they’re made for battle.

In some of the best survivor-like games, the final survivor to unlock can feel underwhelming, but Morvenn lives up to their title all too well. Even though there's only a small number of Adepta Sororitas survivors in the game right now, they’re still almost unstoppable.

#4234. Arc Raiders has proven that extraction shooters can be popular, with over 4 million copies sold in under two weeks

Arc Raiders has sold even more copies, which we should've guessed, given that the game keeps breaking its own concurrent player records.

It’s pretty clear at this stage that Arc Raiders is one of the biggest launches of 2025. More interesting than the numbers themselves, however, is that this is an extraction shooter - a subgenre which has typically been thought of as niche.

If you’ve been paying the PvPvE game any attention, you could easily see how (and why) it keeps breaking its own records.

Today, publisher Nexon announced in a press release (via Gematsu) that Arc Raiders has now sold over 4 million copies. The game came out on October 30, which means it managed to sell that many copies in a little over 10 days.

The news comes on the same day that developer Embark Studios announced that the game had more than 700,000 concurrent players across all platforms over the weekend. Over the same weekend on Steam alone, Arc Raiders broke its own Steam concurrent record with a new peak of 462,488 players - which is a significant chunk of that 700,000+ player base.

This marks the second time the extraction shooter has broken its own concurrent player records, which is something very few games have managed in the past. Arc Raiders remains a top-seller, too. On Steam, it’s currently the second-best seller globally (by revenue), sitting just below Counter-Strike 2.

“The many different ways you play and participate in ARC Raiders have completely blown us away, going far beyond what we ever imagined. You surprise us, you outsmart us, and you keep us on our toes. We wouldn’t have it any other way,” the developer wrote on Twitter.

Embark recently published a roadmap to highlight all the new content coming to the game over the remainder of this year. The first new map is set to arrive this month alongside new Arc units, new gameplay items, new events and more.

Just over the weekend, the game received several new Map Conditions that completely alter the way they play. The developer has already rolled out a couple of updates since launch, in order to tackle exploits and fix a few launchday bugs.

If you’re currently hooked on this gem of a game, we guarantee that our Arc Raiders gameplay tips will have at least one you didn’t know about. We also have more guides on how to find some of the more elusive items in the game, such as olives, lemons and apricots, and prickly pears.

#4233. Arc Raiders' new map will be unlocked through a community event that starts today, and everyone has to donate

It looks like it's going to take the Arc Raiders community a bit of work to unlock the game's next map.

As many of Arc Raiders’ regular players predicted, the game’s first post-launch map won’t just be available for everyone, it will instead be closely tied to a community event. Breaking New Ground is the name of that event, and it’s one where everyone will need to contribute in order to rebuild some old tunnels and unlock the way to Stella Montis.

The event kicks off today alongside the release of the game’s latest patch. The ask is relatively simple: players must commit Basic Materials to the project so that the tunnels can be rebuilt. This option will be available to anyone who’s played at least five rounds.

If you’ve spent any time in Arc Raiders, you’ll know that Basic Materials are things like Metal parts, Fabric, Chemicals, Rubber Parts, and Plastic Parts - most of which are easy to find in the game’s various maps.

Even beyond the ultimate goal of unlocking the new map, donations will also reward you with Merits, which is a new event currency, though there’s a cap on how many you can earn.

Once enough materials have been collected, the next phase of the event, Staking Our Claim, will begin, which will bring a new progression track to the game, and make Stella Montis available for players to visit.

Developer Embark describes the new environment as unlike any that we have seen in the game so far. It’s a facility carved into the northern mountains, which means it’s going to have a near-pristine look; quite the contrast with the rest of the game’s environments.

Stella Montis also has its own Arc enemies, loot, schematics, and other gameplay items. You can look forward to coming across the Shredder, a close-quarter Arc unit exclusive to the new map for now.

Then there’s The Matriarch, a somehow even larger version of the Queen. Thankfully, it will only be available under a specific map condition, so you’re in no danger of running into her randomly. The update will also introduce a new legendary weapon, two new grenades, and three new mines.

Staking Our Claim will only run until December, which is when the next stage of the game’s roadmap will kick off. Then, the Cold Snap update will introduce the Flickering Flames event, the first snowfall Map Condition, and the Expedition Project voluntary wipe.

In case you’re still missing them, here’s how to find lemons and apricots, prickly pear, and olives.

#4232. NASA warns this year's Monster El Niño could be even bigger than legendary 1997 event

NASA scientists are tracking an exceptionally powerful El Niño that could grow even larger than the historic 1997 event, which brought extreme weather to regions around the world. Using 35 years of satellite observations, researchers can now compare the rapidly developing 2026 El Niño with some of the strongest events ever recorded, revealing remarkable similarities and important differences.

El Niño is a recurring climate phenomenon that typically develops every two to seven years, when ocean temperatures rise above normal across parts of the equatorial Pacific. These changes can disrupt atmospheric circulation and alter weather patterns far beyond the Pacific Ocean.

Two of the most powerful recent El Niño events occurred in 1997-98 and 2015-16. Both had widespread consequences, including destructive fires in Indonesia and the Amazon, severe drought and crop failures in southern Africa, and intense rainfall and coastal flooding in Southern California. Now, the 2026 El Niño is emerging as another major event, with satellite data suggesting it could rival those historic episodes.

How El Niño Builds Strength in the Pacific

The development of El Niño depends on a complex interaction between ocean temperatures and atmospheric winds.

Under normal conditions, steady trade winds push warm surface water toward the western Pacific Ocean. This causes warm water to accumulate in the west, where the ocean surface sits slightly higher than it does farther east.

When the trade winds weaken, some of that warm water begins moving eastward across the Pacific. The shift can weaken the winds even further or occasionally cause them to reverse direction. This allows additional warm water to spread east, reinforcing the process and raising ocean temperatures and sea levels across the central and eastern Pacific.

Although the underlying process is similar each time, no two El Niño events develop in exactly the same way. Their behavior depends partly on where the warmest water accumulates and how the atmosphere responds to the changing ocean conditions.

"The search for the 'typical' El Niño is very elusive," said Josh Willis, project scientist for sea level missions at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL). "They're all different in terms of where they land and how their impacts play out."

NASA Satellites Reveal Striking Similarities to 1997

To understand how the current El Niño compares with earlier events, scientists are examining decades of satellite measurements of ocean surface height.

This technique, called satellite altimetry, measures subtle changes in the elevation of the ocean surface. Because seawater expands as it becomes warmer, unusually high sea levels in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific can reveal where heat is accumulating during El Niño.

NASA's comparison maps show differences in Pacific Ocean surface height on October 13, 1997 (left), and October 12, 2026 (right). The earlier measurements were collected by the TOPEX/Poseidon satellite, while the newer observations came from the Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich satellite. Scientists at JPL processed both datasets to make the events easier to compare.

The maps use red to identify areas where the ocean surface is higher than its usual level, while white represents normal conditions and blue shows areas where sea levels are below average. To better isolate the effects of El Niño and other temporary natural changes, researchers removed variations associated with seasonal patterns and long-term trends.

One major advantage of these observations is their remarkable consistency. Successive satellite missions have followed nearly identical paths, with overlapping periods of operation that allow scientists to compare measurements across decades.

"What's unique about altimetry is that we have a 35-year record from nearly identical satellites flying almost the same ground track, with each mission overlapping the next," Willis said. "That lets us look back in time and compare this El Niño to what happened in 1997. And right now, this one is on track to be even bigger."

Why the 2026 El Niño Resembles a Historic Climate Giant

The 2026 El Niño intensified much more abruptly than the powerful 1997-98 event. Despite that difference in timing, NASA's satellite measurements from October reveal striking similarities in how the two events are developing.

In both cases, the Pacific displays a pronounced difference in sea level (low in the west and high in the east). The observations also show elevated, unusually warm water stretching eastward along the equator until it reaches the coast of South America.

These similarities suggest that the 2026 event could produce weather effects resembling those experienced during the 1997-98 El Niño. That earlier episode brought substantial rainfall to California and other parts of the southern United States, raising the possibility of comparable conditions during the coming winter.

However, the powerful 2015-16 El Niño demonstrates why similarities in overall strength do not necessarily translate into identical weather impacts.

For that comparison, NASA scientists also examined ocean surface height measurements from October 12, 2015, recorded by the Jason-2 satellite. The data were placed alongside observations from approximately the same time of year in 1997 and 2026.

Although the 2015 event also featured exceptionally warm water and elevated sea levels along the equator, that warm water did not extend toward the South American coast as strongly as it did during the other two events.

The resulting rainfall patterns were different as well. During the winter of 2015-16, much of the precipitation associated with El Niño was concentrated over Central America and the southeastern United States, while Mexico experienced significant flooding.

Will El Niño Bring Extreme Weather in Winter 2026-27?

The latest observations have prompted scientists to closely monitor how the 2026 El Niño develops and what it could mean for weather conditions in the months ahead.

In its October 8, 2026, outlook, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) estimated an 83 percent chance that strong to very strong El Niño conditions would occur during the first three months of 2027.

That forecast points to the potential for a particularly significant climate event, but it does not establish exactly where the most severe effects will occur.

El Niño can influence weather across much of the planet by changing the movement of heat and moisture through the atmosphere. However, those effects become increasingly difficult to predict farther from the tropical Pacific, where other atmospheric processes can alter or weaken the expected patterns.

As a result, even the strong resemblance between the 2026 and 1997 events cannot guarantee that the coming winter will unfold in the same way.

"There's always a bit of a dice roll here," Willis said. "Just because this El Niño looks like 1997 doesn't mean it will be exactly the same -- it's just our best guess at the moment."

The unprecedented consistency of the satellite record gives researchers a valuable way to recognize familiar patterns and evaluate the scale of the developing El Niño. But whether 2026-27 ultimately matches the extreme weather of previous historic events will depend on how the ocean and atmosphere interact in the months ahead.

#4231. Aurora Gaming sweep Pixel Lumina to reach Europe Qualifier 1 final after BONK disqualification

Aurora Gaming beat Pixel Lumina 2-0 to reach the Europe Qualifier 1 final, days after the UK side that had knocked them out was disqualified for cheating. The final decides seeding for the Europe Qualifier Playoffs, the next step towards VCT EMEA Kickoff 2027 in Berlin.

Aurora Gaming will play in the Europe Qualifier 1 final. Their best-of-three semi-final against Pixel Lumina began at 16:00 on Tuesday. Aurora took the opening map in 41 minutes and closed out the second in 35 minutes.

The win completes a turnaround for a side that had already been eliminated from the qualifier. Their earlier exit had come against BONK.

The fallout reached beyond the bracket. Every BONK player and registered participant was also provisionally suspended, GINX TV reported.

The disqualification forced a rework of the schedule. Riot had set Qualifier 1 for 5 to 8 November as a single-elimination, best-of-three bracket. The Pixel Lumina semi-final and the final were pushed back to make room for the rebuilt bracket. All three affected organisations agreed to the new timetable.

Pixel Lumina, a team based in Hungary, came into the match at rank 120 in the Elo power rankings. They hold a rating of 1559 and a 30-28 record across 58 rated matches. Aurora are unranked. Before this semi-final, Pixel Lumina lost to CGN Esports in the VCL EMEA Last Chance Qualifier 2026. That defeat followed wins over FOKUS and Twisted Saints Esports in the same event.

Aurora’s lineup features Boo, chiwa, Derke, B1SK and trexx. Derke joined straight after Valorant Champions 2026, where his Vitality side lost the grand final 3-1 to LOUD.

Aurora now face the winner of xXxMasterProMegaTeamxXx versus F9 EICAR. That final decides seeding for the Kickoff Qualifier Playoffs. Aurora are already listed as qualified for the playoffs through Qualifier 1, so the final is about position rather than survival.

The wider prize is a place at VCT EMEA Kickoff 2027. Europe will supply half of the four non-partner sides heading to the event, Riot Games said, while Türkiye and MENA each send a single team. Kickoff itself will be played offline at the Riot Games Arena in Berlin with 12 teams.

The rest of the European field is still taking shape. Europe Qualifier 2 is scheduled for 12 to 15 November and is also played as single-elimination best-of-three brackets.

Version 2.4’s biggest claim to fame is the introduction of the Krampus Compliance Authority, a new faction that’s affiliated with TOPS. This looks to be the oversight committee, dispatched after the squad’s adventure beneath Timesworn Hill.

The events of this narrative arch follow on from the Timesworn Hill crisis, which is partly why we’re going to a new area as part of this update. The old mining site can now be explored for the first time in a decade, now that the Miasma has begun to recede.

#4229. MIT scientists discover a surprising way to boost the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

While we go about our daily activities, the brain gradually accumulates waste, including lactic acid and proteins that are no longer useful. Sleep provides an important opportunity to clear away these substances. As we rest, waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) move through the brain, helping remove waste and maintain healthy brain function.

Researchers at MIT have now discovered a way to make these fluid waves stronger using brief pulses of a gentle sound called "pink noise." When delivered at carefully chosen moments during sleep, the sounds amplify slow electrical waves in the brain. Those stronger electrical signals, in turn, produce larger waves of CSF.

The finding opens up intriguing possibilities for improving brain health. Scientists want to determine whether increasing this fluid movement could sharpen thinking, strengthen memory, or slow neurodegenerative diseases associated with the accumulation of damaging proteins, including amyloid beta.

"We found that we were able to increase the size of the CSF flow wave during sleep, which as far as we know, there hasn't been a method to do before. Now that we can enhance CSF flow during sleep in healthy adults, we're really excited to bring this technology to clinical populations to see what effects we can have," says Laura Lewis, the Athinoula A. Martinos Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, a member of MIT's Institute for Medical Engineering and Science and the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and an associate member of the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory.

Lewis led the research as senior author. The findings were published in Science Translational Medicine, with Joshua Levitt serving as lead author. Levitt recently completed his PhD at Boston University and previously worked as a visiting graduate student in Lewis' laboratory.

Cerebrospinal fluid is a transparent liquid that surrounds the brain and spinal cord, providing protection against physical injury. It also supports brain function by transporting nutrients, including glucose, and carrying away waste released by brain cells as they consume energy.

In 2019, Lewis demonstrated that functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) could be used to observe the movement of CSF into and out of the brain during sleep. Her team found that this movement closely follows slow electrical brain waves, which are especially prominent during deep sleep.

Building on that discovery, the researchers wanted to understand whether deliberately strengthening these electrical waves would also increase the movement of CSF. Earlier experiments had shown that sounds presented at precisely the right moment could enhance slow brain waves.

"You can make more of these electrical slow waves through an auditory stimulus, if it comes at just the right time. Similar to a child on a swing, if you push them when they're at the right moment in their movement, you can make that swing go farther," Lewis says. "The challenge is: How do you find just the right time?"

To test the idea, the team used extremely short bursts of pink noise, each lasting just 50 milliseconds. Pink noise contains the full range of frequencies that humans can hear, much like white noise. However, its lower frequencies are more prominent, while higher frequencies are quieter. The result is a softer, more balanced sound reminiscent of steady rainfall or a waterfall heard from a distance.

Timing was essential. The researchers needed to deliver each burst of sound when a sleeping participant's slow brain waves reached their peak. To identify those moments, they monitored electrical activity using EEG while simultaneously measuring CSF movement with fMRI.

Combining the two measurements created a technical obstacle. The powerful magnetic fields used in fMRI interfere with EEG recordings, making it difficult to detect the brain's electrical signals accurately and quickly enough to synchronize the sound.

The team addressed this problem by creating a method that removes interference from EEG signals in less than 100 milliseconds. They also designed an algorithm capable of predicting when the next slow wave peak would occur, compensating for the small delay introduced by processing the signals. Together, these advances made it possible to play each burst of pink noise at the intended moment.

Stronger Brain Cleaning Waves During Sleep

The researchers tested their approach in 14 healthy volunteers. They found that the carefully timed sounds increased the size of both the brain's slow electrical waves and the accompanying CSF waves. Importantly, the sounds were quiet enough that they did not wake the participants.

The brain scans also helped explain how the process works. Slow electrical waves were associated with blood vessels narrowing and widening, creating a pumping effect that pushes CSF out of the brain. These slow waves occur during non-REM sleep and become increasingly pronounced as sleep deepens.

By enhancing the electrical waves, the researchers were able to strengthen the fluid movement associated with the brain's natural waste removal process. However, the study did not directly establish whether the stronger CSF waves actually removed more waste or improved sleep quality.

Could Pink Noise Improve Sleep and Help Fight Alzheimer's?

The researchers now want to investigate whether increasing CSF flow leads to more refreshing, restorative sleep, particularly for people who struggle with insomnia. Another major goal is to determine whether the technique can improve the brain's ability to clear harmful substances.

This possibility is especially relevant to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia, which are associated with the accumulation of abnormal proteins in the brain. If stronger CSF movement ultimately translates into more effective waste removal, the approach could offer a new way to address one of the biological processes involved in these conditions.

"Brain waste clearance is really important for Alzheimer's and other forms of dementia, which are caused, in part, by the buildup of molecules like amyloid and tau in the brain. If we can improve brain waste clearance, we may be able to help prevent the buildups of these plaques that lead to disease," Levitt says.

The technology could eventually become accessible outside research laboratories. Levitt has launched a company that aims to develop a home device, potentially in the form of a headband, that would deliver sound at the appropriate moments during sleep to increase CSF flow.

For now, the results demonstrate that a simple auditory stimulus, when precisely synchronized with brain activity, can alter the fluid waves associated with the brain's nighttime cleaning process. Whether those changes can translate into better sleep, stronger memory, or protection against neurodegenerative disease remains an important question for future studies.

The research received funding from a McKnight Scholar Award, a Sloan Fellowship, a Pew Biomedical Scholars Award, the Simons Foundation Collaboration on Plasticity in the Aging Brain, the MIT EECS Transformative Research Fund, the National Institutes of Health, the Corundum Convergence Institute, and the Panasonic Well Fellowship for AI and Wellness.

#4228. Forget Ganon, This Is What’s Actually Killing Players in Ocarina of Time Remake

Covering the video games industry since 2017, with experience in news, articles, and reviews. Currently a writer at DualShockers and gaming magazines.

You'd think that after spending dozens of hours exploring Hyrule, fighting terrifying monsters, and eventually taking on Ganondorf himself, players would have some pretty impressive causes of death in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake.

Well, think again! Thanks to the game's new Zelda Notes companion, we can now see what has been giving players the most trouble, and some of these statistics are honestly hilarious.

Released alongside the remake, Zelda Notes is a feature within the Nintendo Switch app designed to accompany players on their adventures. It offers a real-time map, additional lore, a photo editor, daily activity summaries, and, perhaps most interestingly, personal and global gameplay statistics. And while these numbers are still evolving as more people play, they've already revealed a few amusing details about the community.

According to these global statistics on November 11, Big Skulltulas are currently the most defeated enemies in the game, accounting for 15% of all recorded kills. Stalchild, Tektites, and Keese share second place with 8% each – considering how often these creatures appear while freely exploring Hyrule, those numbers aren't particularly surprising.

The causes of death, however, are a different story! You might expect players to lose most of their hearts against a difficult temple boss or during the final showdown with Ganondorf. Nope – the biggest culprit is actually ReDeads and Gibdos, responsible for 18% of recorded deaths.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake has finally been released, and fans have already discovered several game-breaking glitches.

And honestly, I can't blame anyone for that one! These enemies are already pretty terrifying, but their increased speed in the remake makes encounters with them considerably more dangerous. Getting caught by one can quickly turn into a nightmare, especially if you're not prepared.

The second most common cause of death is more embarrassing, though: fire. Yes, just fire. Not a particularly powerful enemy or a complicated boss encounter, but simply getting burned by environmental hazards. I'm sorry if you contributed to that statistic, but I can't help finding it funny!

You might expect players to lose most of their hearts against a difficult temple boss or during the final showdown with Ganondorf. Nope – the biggest culprit is actually ReDeads and Gibdos, responsible for 18% of recorded deaths.

At least the third most common cause is a little more respectable. Iron Knuckles, which serve as challenging miniboss encounters, have also claimed plenty of victims. Losing a fight against one is certainly easier to forgive than walking into a flame.

The companion's statistics also track what causes damage without necessarily resulting in a Game Over. Environmental traps, including moving hazards found throughout temples, are responsible for 9% of recorded damage, while ReDeads and Gibdos come in second with 7%.

Some of the original's most charming quirks from Zelda: Ocarina of Time didn't make the journey.

Thankfully, not every statistic is quite so grim. The Hookshot is currently the most-used weapon, accounting for 31% of player usage, while the Lens of Truth dominates the magic item category with 40%. That second result isn't particularly shocking, considering how essential the item is for certain sections of the adventure.

Finally, Zelda Notes reveals that most players are taking between 20 and 30 hours to complete Ocarina of Time. That's a pretty reasonable amount of time for such a beloved adventure, although I apparently took things a little more slowly. My own playthrough lasted around 45 hours, so I guess I really wanted to savour every moment in Hyrule!

Either way, these statistics are a fun reminder that even after all these years, Ocarina of Time can still surprise us. And if you're currently playing the remake, maybe keep an eye out for those ReDeads. Ganondorf might be the big bad, but he's clearly not the one you should be worrying about most.

Link has always been known as the silent hero of Hyrule, but the remake appears to have given him a very brief spoken line.

#4227. Scientists discover that the heart doesn't age the way we thought

As the heart gets older, inflammation increases, but scientists have not fully understood where these changes occur or which parts of the organ are most affected. Researchers at The Jackson Laboratory (JAX) have now uncovered a surprising pattern: Certain regions of the heart appear to be hotspots for aging-related inflammation, offering new clues about how the heart changes over time.

In a study of mouse hearts published in Aging Cell, the researchers discovered that signs of inflammation and tissue scarring were especially concentrated around the aortic valves and aortic root. These areas contain immune cells and connective tissue cells whose interactions change with age, potentially affecting the surrounding heart muscle. The findings provide a new picture of cardiac aging and could guide future efforts to understand cardiovascular disease.

"Some of the markers associated with inflammaging were there from the very beginning in young hearts, but they were focused specifically in areas no one had defined before, in the valves and the aorta rather than in muscle tissue," said study author Nadia Rosenthal, scientific director at JAX. "We really have to think of aging as something that is not linear, because just like we know that people don't age at the same rate, what we know now is that organs and tissues don't age at the same rate either, even within one individual."

Much of the previous research on heart aging has centered on cardiac muscle, particularly the left ventricle. This chamber performs the essential task of pumping blood into the aorta and throughout the body. By studying the heart as a whole, rather than concentrating primarily on its muscle, the JAX team uncovered important changes in other tissues and the ways their cells interact.

"The valves and the major blood vessels are parts often thought of as plumbing rather than the main engine, but this is a very complicated little machine," Rosenthal said. "It turns out they're home to many of the cells we're interested in, and that's where some of the most important aging-related signals were concentrated."

Growing older is the single greatest risk factor for cardiovascular disease, yet many of the cellular processes responsible for the heart's decline remain poorly understood. One challenge is that mammalian heart muscle cells have very little ability to regenerate or replace themselves. To investigate what happens as the heart ages, Rosenthal and her colleagues used advanced techniques that allowed them to study thousands of individual cells from young and old mice while also identifying their locations within the heart.

Scientists already know that aging is accompanied by a persistent, low level of inflammation throughout the body. Earlier studies have found similar changes in the heart, including an increase in immune cells that regulate inflammatory activity (macrophages) and cells that produce and maintain connective tissue and contribute to scar formation (fibroblasts).

The new analysis showed that aging macrophages became more active in genes involved in inflammation and changes to tissue structure. Fibroblasts, meanwhile, increasingly displayed molecular characteristics associated with fibrosis (or scarring). Crucially, the researchers went beyond identifying which genes were active. They also mapped the locations of these cells, making it possible to see how different regions of the heart change as they grow older.

This approach revealed that inflammation and fibrosis (or scarring) were not distributed uniformly. Instead, the strongest signals appeared around the heart valves and aortic root. The researchers believe these regions may act as important centers of cardiac aging, where changes in supporting cells could influence the health of nearby heart muscle.

"To keep muscle cells happy, the other cells in the heart have to continue supporting them throughout life," Rosenthal said. "What this study does, for the first time, is provide a comprehensive picture of how those support cells, particularly fibroblasts and macrophages, change with age and contribute to what we call inflammaging."

Surprising Signs of Aging in Young Hearts

Another unexpected discovery challenged assumptions about how scientists identify aging cells. The team examined molecular markers frequently associated with cellular senescence, a state in which cells permanently lose the ability to divide, often because of aging or stress. As senescent cells accumulate, they can contribute to ongoing inflammation, tissue damage, and diseases associated with older age.

Surprisingly, some of these supposedly age-related markers were already present in young mouse hearts. Their presence suggests that the markers alone cannot reliably establish whether a cell has entered senescence, and that their meaning may depend on where they appear and the condition of the surrounding tissue.

"What surprised us was that some of these markers that have been associated with aging were already present in young hearts. They weren't where anyone expected to find them, and that forced us to rethink what those markers are telling us," Rosenthal said. "That turns the usual interpretation of cardiac aging on its ear because these markers alone don't mean a cell is senescent. There's nothing senescent about a six-month-old mouse heart."

The researchers also identified genes that became more active with age and were especially prominent in the same regions. Among them were Ccl8, which helps transmit inflammatory signals, and Cdkn1a (also known as p21), a gene widely used as an indicator of cellular senescence. Their locations provided further evidence that the valves and aortic root may be particularly important areas for understanding how the heart ages.

"We're not talking about single genes. We're talking about an entire conversation between immune cells and fibroblasts. As the heart ages, the way those cells communicate changes, and that shift appears to be linked to the inflammation and tissue remodeling we see in older hearts," Rosenthal said.

Male and Female Hearts Show Different Aging Patterns

The study uncovered another important distinction: Aging did not produce exactly the same molecular changes in male and female mouse hearts.

In males, aging fibroblasts showed stronger connections to biological processes associated with fibrosis. In females, the corresponding changes were more closely related to pathways involved in heart development and protein production.

Rosenthal noted that these differences may offer clues about cardiovascular aging in humans. Heart disease tends to become more common in women after menopause, while its development in men generally follows a more gradual pattern. The distinct cellular changes observed in male and female mice could help researchers investigate the biological processes behind these differences.

However, the results describe differences in molecular activity, not demonstrated differences in heart function or disease risk. Further research will be needed to determine how these patterns influence cardiovascular health.

To explore whether their findings might also apply to people, the team compared the mouse results with previously published data from human hearts. Several molecular processes associated with aging, including pathways involved in responding to cellular stress, appeared in both species. This overlap suggests that at least some of the biological changes identified in mice may also be relevant to human heart aging.

"Our findings change the focus from aging across the entire heart to specific anatomical hotspots, helping us better understand how inflammation and fibrosis are connected and which regions of the heart are involved in the aging process," said study author Amalia Sintou, a postdoctoral associate at JAX.

Could These Discoveries Help Protect Aging Hearts?

Although the research does not yet identify a new treatment, it offers scientists a more detailed understanding of where aging-related changes occur and which cells are involved. By revealing these cellular patterns, the findings could help guide future studies aimed at reducing cardiovascular decline, maintaining healthy heart function, and improving health later in life.

Rosenthal's team is now examining whether exercise, diet, and disease alter the interactions between immune cells and connective tissue cells. The researchers hope to distinguish the normal effects of aging from changes that may leave the heart increasingly vulnerable to cardiovascular problems.

The experimental design also helped the team isolate aging itself as a contributing factor. Because the mice lived under the same conditions and received the same diet, the researchers could investigate age-related changes without the additional variation introduced by different environments or eating habits.

"Valve replacement is common in older adults, and one of the big questions is how much of the underlying damage is driven by aging itself," said study author Aleksandra Aljakna Khan, a postdoctoral associate at JAX. "Because all of the mice in our study lived in the same environment and ate the same diet, we were able to isolate the effects of aging and show that aging alone can initiate some of these changes in the valves and aorta."

Together, the findings suggest that understanding heart aging requires looking beyond the muscle responsible for pumping blood. The valves, major blood vessels, and supporting cells may play a much larger role than previously recognized. Learning how these structures change and communicate over time could eventually help scientists identify ways to preserve cardiovascular health as people age.

The research received funding from the NIH Common Fund through The Jackson Laboratory Senescence Tissue Mapping Center (JAX-Sen TMC U54 AG079753). Additional support came from JAX's National Cancer Institute-designated Cancer Center (P30 CA034196).

Additional authors from The Jackson Laboratory included Yue Zhao, Antonios Somarakis, Harshpreet Chandok, Juliana Alcoforado Diniz, Ramalakshmi Ramasamy, Gretchen T. Clark, Brian S. White, Paul Robson, Ron Korstanje, and J. Matthew Mahoney. Leon Frommer and Sikander Hayat of RWTH Aachen University also contributed to the study.

#4226. Battlefield 6 gets a new map today alongside major changes to controller aim assist, and even more weapon dispersion tweaks

Right on schedule, the latest Battlefield 6 patch has arrived to kick off the next stage of Season 1.

Battlefield 6’s first season has entered its second phase. The game received a major update earlier today, version 1.1.2.0, which delivers a host of changes to the game, many of which have been expected.

The update, of course, also adds new content to the game in the form of the map Eastwood, as well as new hardware and fresh features for the multiplayer sandbox.

We’ve known about the new content side of today’s patch for quite some time. The update kicks off the California Resistance stage of Season 1, which is the second of three. The new Eastwood map takes place in California, and it’s a map cut from the larger Battlefield Redsec battle royale map of Fort Lyndon.

There’s a new limited-time mode called Sabotage - a tactical, 8v8 mode where two teams attempt to destroy as many bomb sites as possible. The other big new feature that arrives today is Battle Pickups.

These are powerful weapons which can be found in specific game modes (and in Portal), scattered around the map for players to pick up and use. They have limited ammo that cannot be replenished, and deliver incredible firepower.

Redsec players have a new Gauntlet mission to look forward to that joins the existing modes. It’s called Rodeo and it involves a lot of vehicular action. Finally, everyone gets to unlock two new weapons: the the DB-12 shotgun, and the M327 Trait revolver sidearm. There’s also a new angled grip attachment.

The fixes and tweaks side of the patch is arguably the more interesting. Controller aim assist has received a big overhaul that essentially resets everything to open beta settings. The goal is to make infantry targeting more consistent.

Controller players actually get the bulk of the changes in this update, which also improves input latency and stick response. Several issues that reset aim assist values, or make it behave erratically, have been addressed.

The conversation around weapon bloom/spread doesn’t look like it’s ever going to end, because Battlefield Studios is yet again tuning gunplay to fix unintended dispersion behaviour, and decrease its intensity across the board.

Certain Challenges have had their description rewritten so their requirements can be better understood. Beyond that, you can expect several deployables to behave much more consistently, including several bug fixes there, too.

Head to the official blog for the full rundown of patch 1.1.2.0.

#4225. Vitamin B12 may hold the key to treating a rare genetic disorder

A surprising discovery involving vitamin B12 could open new possibilities for understanding and potentially treating rare genetic disorders. Researchers found that the vitamin can correct developmental problems in tiny worms carrying a genetic mutation associated with Verheij syndrome, a rare human condition that causes developmental delays, impaired growth, and short stature.

The findings center on a cellular process called RNA splicing, which helps prepare the genetic instructions cells use to produce proteins. During splicing, unnecessary portions of messenger RNA are removed, and the remaining sections are joined together in the correct order. When this process goes wrong, it can disrupt essential cellular functions and contribute to serious developmental disorders.

Mutations in genes responsible for splicing can cause conditions such as Verheij syndrome. To better understand the effects of these genetic changes, scientists investigated how a related mutation affects growth and metabolism in a laboratory model.

Vitamin B12 Reverses Developmental Defects in Worms

The discovery emerged from experiments involving C. elegans, a tiny roundworm commonly used in biological research. The researchers were initially searching for previously unknown genes that influence lifespan when they began examining a mutation in a gene involved in RNA splicing. The same gene is associated with Verheij syndrome in humans.

Worms carrying the mutation developed problems resembling important features of the human disorder. Their growth slowed considerably, and they remained smaller than normal.

To investigate why this happened, the scientists conducted genetic screens and analyzed the worms' metabolism. They discovered that the mutation disrupted specific metabolic pathways that depend on vitamin B12 and are essential for healthy growth and normal cellular activity.

The researchers then tested whether providing additional vitamin B12 could counteract these changes. Remarkably, the treatment restored the affected metabolic processes to normal and corrected the developmental abnormalities associated with the mutation.

"We were surprised to find that a change in a fundamental process of RNA processing had such a targeted effect on vitamin B12-dependent metabolism," says Jonathan Kölschbach, first author of the study. "Even more exciting was that we were able to largely correct the consequences of this change in the worm model using vitamin B12."

Could Vitamin B12 Help Treat a Rare Genetic Disorder?

To explore whether their findings might also apply to people, the researchers examined publicly available datasets from human cells. They also worked with Hormos Dafsari, a neuropediatrician at the University Hospital Cologne, to collect blood samples from patients diagnosed with Verheij syndrome.

These investigations uncovered evidence of similar metabolic changes in humans, suggesting that the vitamin B12-related pathways affected in the worms may also play a role in the human disorder.

Although the results are promising, researchers have not yet established whether vitamin B12 supplementation can improve symptoms in people with Verheij syndrome. Additional studies will be necessary to determine whether the benefits observed in worms can be translated into a treatment for patients.

The discovery also raises a broader possibility. Metabolic disruptions may contribute more substantially to diseases caused by faulty RNA splicing than scientists previously recognized. Understanding these connections could help researchers identify new therapeutic strategies, potentially extending beyond Verheij syndrome to other rare genetic conditions.

"Our study is a good example of how basic research on model organisms can provide new insights into human diseases," says Adam Antebi, Director at the Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing and lead author of the study. "A fundamental biological question can thus give rise to a new approach that could also become medically relevant in the long term."

#4224. Battlefield 6 is getting a free trial next week with... a questionable selection of maps, but at least the modes are good

If Redsec got you hooked on Battlefield gameplay but you never experienced traditional multiplayer in Battlefield 6, there's an upcoming moment you might want to pay attention to.

Presumably as a way of marching ever forward towards its (alleged) 100 million player goal for Battlefield 6, EA has announced that the multiplayer shooter will be getting its first free trial later this month.

This is, of course, specifically for players to sample the core, paid component of the game, as the recently launched Redsec remains free-to-play. Redsec, however, offers modes like battle royale and Gauntlet, which aren’t quite the traditional Battlefield experience.

The Battlefield 6 trial arrives next Tuesday, November 25. It will run for one week, ending the following Tuesday, December 2. The trial will be available on all platforms, but won’t include all content from the full game.

Instead, players will have access to three of the game’s maps and five of its modes. Siege of Cairo will be there alongside Season 1’s two new maps: Eastwood, and Blackwell Fields. It’s not the strongest line-up of maps, considering Eastwood is already cut from the larger Fort Lyndon battle royale map that Redsec players should be quite familiar with, but it’s something.

As for modes, you can pick from Conquest, Breakthrough, Sabotage, and Team Deathmatch. Battlefield Studios didn’t say what the fifth mode is going to be, but a dedicated blog post with more information is set to arrive next week.

Beyond the trial's content itself, the timing is certainly great. Battlefield 6 just received one of its biggest patches, kicking off the second phase of its first season. So far this season, we’ve seen two new maps, several new weapons - but more importantly, solutions to problems the game’s had since launch, as well as fixes to longstanding bugs.

The miserable XP progression Battlefield 6 launched with is far more tolerable. Challenges and Assignments are much easier to understand and actually finish. The often maligned weapon dispersion has been toned down. Some of the wildest vehicle bugs have been fixed. And Portal has a host of experiences that go beyond just bot farms.

In essence, Battlefield 6 feels like its reached its 1.0 status, which makes this a great entry point for new players, even if the trial could've used more of the game's better maps.
