#4144. Cover Reveal – Tomb Raider: Legacy Of Atlantis

Game Informer’s next cover story is Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis, the upcoming reimagining of the original 1996 Tomb Raider arriving on February 12. Since that game celebrates the franchise’s 30th anniversary this year, we’re doing the same with a double-whammy of Tomb Raider features.

We visited Crystal Dynamics’ office to play Legacy of Atlantis for several hours, including an exclusive tour of the Greece section. For our 12-page cover story, we spoke to key team members at Crystal Dynamics and Flying Wild Hog to learn why it’s tackling Lara Croft’s seminal adventure once again (having already remade the game once in Tomb Raider: Anniversary), how this version of the game differs from previous incarnations and why, discuss the teams' controversial use of AI development tools, and how Legacy of Atlantis plants seeds for the upcoming Tomb Raider: Catalyst.

The issue also includes a six-page retrospective of Tomb Raider’s 30-year history, with insights from Crystal Dynamics. This celebration is reflected in our cover art, designed by Tomb Raider franchise art director Brenoch Adams, which showcases every version of Lara Croft from the Core Design, Legend, Survivor, and current eras.

The December issue also marks the return of our annual (and very large) holiday buyers guide, featuring curated gift suggestions for the gamers in your life ahead of the winter holidays. Furthermore, we’ve created a list of family-friendly games to enjoy with younger relatives during upcoming holiday gatherings. Guest contributor Veerender Singh Jubbal writes about India's emerging game development scene and how its community is helping elevate local titles to an international stage. Ahead of the launch of Ryu Ga Gatoku’s Stranger Than Heaven, executive editor Brian Shea played a new section of the era-spanning Yakuza/Like a Dragon prequel while picking the brains of its lead designers for details on the game’s plot, themes, and time periods. Senior associate editor Wesley LeBlanc shares his glowing impressions of Murals, the colorful, fairy-tale-inspired adventure from Disney Illusion Island developer Dlala Studios, whom he spoke with about the game’s conception.

We also have plenty of previews for upcoming games including Final Fantasy VII Revelation, Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV, Muramasa: Revenant Blades, Fate/Extra Record, Tiny Metal 2, Mr. Records, and Eternal Anima. We also have reviews for Gears of War: E-Day, Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse, Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve, Control Resonant, Star Wars: Galactic Racer, Silent Hill: Downfall, and many more.

#4143. Brawlhalla set to collaborate with My Hero Academia as Izuki Midoriya and co join the brawl

Say what you like about Brawlhalla, but Ubisoft's Smash-like fighting game has chugged along quite nicely whereas other crossover-focused fighters like Multiversus have flagged. Now, Brawlhalla is reaching outside their usual crop of guest fighters to bring in the cast of none other than My Hero Academia!

#4142. Legendary game creator Vince Zampella has passed away

Vince Zampella, co-creator of Call of Duty, and a veteran studio head responsible for some of the biggest franchises in the world, is gone.

Vince Zampella, known for co-creating the Call of Duty series, among many other roles, has died. Zampella, 55, died in a car crash in Los Angeles on Sunday. The fatal crash killed him, along with the occupant of his car.

According to NBC, Zampella’s Ferrari hit a concrete barrier after leaving a tunnel in the San Gabriel Mountains, north of Los Angeles. Zampella was unfortunately trapped in an ensuing car fire, and the passenger was ejected.

Vince Zampella is one of the industry’s most prolific creators. His storied career is long, and is responsible for some of the biggest shooter franchises in history. It started with Medal of Honor in the 90s, a game that changed WW2 shooters forever.

Zampella later co-founded the legendary Infinity Ward in 2002, the team that would go on to redefine multiplayer shooters forever. Infinity Ward is the studio responsible for the Call of Duty series, which remains one of the biggest games for publisher Activision, and the entire industry.

Zampella then left the studio he founded in 2010 following a major fallout with Activision. He, along with longtime collaborator, Jason West, went to rival publisher EA to form Respawn Entertainment.

Respawn went on to create the Titanfall series, and later Apex Legends. The studio is responsible for non-shooters, of course, like the third-person action game series Star Wars Jedi. Zampella was instrumental in making the game possible, having hired God of War 3 director Stig Asmussen to helm a team within Respawn out of a desire to diversify the studio’s output and prove he can do more than make shooters.

Zampella had only recently met with journalists and peers at The Game Awards, where Battlefield 6 was nominated for multiple awards. Battlefield 6 is the most successful game in series history, in part as a result of Zampella’s leadership. The legendary leader was given the reigns of the struggling multiplayer shooter franchise in 2021, with a goal of finding a viable future.

Zampella’s sudden death has shaken the industry, and many mourn his loss as the news started spreading.

“We are heartbroken by the loss of Vince Zampella, a creative leader whose work shaped generations of players and helped define what modern shooters and action games could be,” EA said in a statement.

“While his impact reached far beyond any one game or studio, we will remember Vince for how he showed up every day, trusting his teams, encouraging bold ideas, and believing in Battlefield and the people building it. We are deeply grateful for his leadership, his generosity, and the care he brought to everything he touched, and we will carry that forward with us.”

#4140. Ocarina of Time Remake Actually Shows Its Entire Story Before Link's Adventure Begins

Covering the video games industry since 2017, with experience in news, articles, and reviews. Currently a writer at DualShockers and gaming magazines.

One of the best things about revisiting a game like The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is discovering little details you might have missed the first time around. The remake has already given fans plenty of reasons to explore every corner of Hyrule again, but one particularly interesting discovery might have been hiding in plain sight from the very beginning.

When visiting Princess Zelda for the first time as Child Link, players can spot a tapestry inside one of the windows in Hyrule Castle's courtyard. And this tapestry actually depicts the entire story of the remake, including events that players are only supposed to see after completing the adventure.

Even stranger, this is the same tapestry that can be unlocked through the game's Threads of Time feature after finishing the main story. In other words, the game is showing you the full journey before Link even takes his first steps toward becoming the Hero of Time!

Link has always been known as the silent hero of Hyrule, but the remake appears to have given him a very brief spoken line.

You just need to move the camera in the right direction to catch it (thankfully, the remake's new dedicated camera controls make that little discovery much easier). Here, take a look for yourself: see the tapestry in the original Reddit post.

This discovery is particularly interesting when you consider what happened in the Nintendo 3DS version of Ocarina of Time. Back then, the same window featured a mural referencing The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword, serving both as a bit of cross-promotion and a way to connect the lore of the two games. The remake, however, has replaced that reference with something much more specific to the adventure we're playing.

When visiting Princess Zelda for the first time as Child Link, players can spot a tapestry inside one of the windows in Hyrule Castle's courtyard.

And naturally, fans haven't wasted any time coming up with explanations! One of the most popular theories suggests that the tapestry is further evidence that we're literally reliving the legend of the Hero of Time. After all, if the entire story is already depicted inside the castle, perhaps the events of Ocarina of Time are not simply unfolding for the first time. They're a story that Hyrule's people already know, one that keeps being told and experienced across generations.

Others have taken the discovery as a reason to look at the game's story from a different perspective. If the Royal Family knew what was coming, perhaps they also knew that Ganondorf would eventually be defeated by the Hero of Time. In that case, accepting the events as they were foretold might have seemed safer than trying to interfere with a fate they believed was already written.

Nintendo has expanded one of the original Zelda: Ocarina of Time's most heartbreaking side stories.

But that interpretation also raises an amusing question: why does Zelda still tell Link that her father doesn't believe Ganondorf is up to no good? I mean, he may not completely believe her, but the tapestry clearly shows the Gerudo king's eventual transformation into a monstrous beast and his attempt to kill both Link and Zelda! You'd think that would be enough to convince the king to be a little more suspicious.

Either way, we have another theory, which is probably the most creative and crazy one (so, naturally, also my personal favorite). Some players believe that the tapestry appears unusually far to the left inside the castle corridor, leaving what looks like plenty of empty wall space beside it. And if you've been following the community's ongoing hunt for clues about a potential Majora's Mask remake, you can probably guess where this is going!

Yes, some fans believe that the empty space is intentional, potentially leaving room for more tapestries depicting other legendary adventures. The next one could very well represent Majora's Mask, especially if Nintendo is planning another remake using the same approach as Ocarina of Time.

Of course, there's no confirmation that this is what Nintendo has in mind, and an empty wall is hardly definitive evidence of another Zelda remake. Still, I can't help but love the idea that this seemingly harmless decoration is actually a little tease of what's coming next!

#4138. Void/Breaker Review – Chaos Is The Point

Many games tout impressive destruction systems under the hood, but few implement it as well as Void/Breaker. The ruin is visually spectacular, sure – who doesn’t love to watch buildings crumble because of your grenade or gravity-thrown explosives? But importantly, it’s a critical aspect of Void/Breaker’s roguelite design. Enemies caught beneath falling rubble become instantly staggered, and that’s your moment to kill. Grenades do this too, as do most items you throw at the hostile AI machinery trying to end your run, creating a vortex of shifting priorities as you dash, jump, and shoot at sequential staggered enemies in your sightlines. Countless weapon mods and permutations make fewer than a dozen weapons feel like hundreds in your arsenal, adding even more blissful chaos to the mix. Though it can be difficult at times, if you can see through the literal remains of your destruction, one of the year’s most engaging shooters awaits.

Void/Breaker wastes no time getting a gun in your hand. An AI voice in your head wants your help escaping a simulation where thousands of runners attempt to reach the end of multi-arena stages to defeat a boss. He asks that you simply follow the simulation’s commands; meanwhile, he uses the data you collect along the way to find new exits for you and him. The storytelling style is very reminiscent of Valve’s Portal. Something much larger is at play here, but it’s worth discovering for yourself.

This narrative framework supports the game’s roguelite structure. Mechanically, however, you enter various themed digital stages, from liminal spaces to beaches to snow-capped cliffs and more, and attempt to survive. Most arenas consist of a couple of starkly white structures that your grenades and thrown explosives can topple (ideally onto waves of enemies below). Learning the language of Void/Breaker means constantly scanning your field of view for explosives and structures practically begging to come down, and then eyeing neon-green bars above enemies that tell you they’re staggered and ready for a quick kill. Developer Stubby Games throws plenty of wrenches into this formula, like armored foes and electrostatic enemies you must melee first, and elite bots that will have you on the back foot, but for the most part, Void/Breaker’s formula is “Break stuff, then kill.”

The game emphasizes explosives and bringing buildings down, but your guns do most of the killing; you can only select one weapon per run. You choose from a pistol, shotgun, machine gun, sniper, and more, and each has its perks (though once I unlocked the SMG, I rarely picked anything else). There’s no sense overthinking your weapon, though, because the dozens of mods you pick up each run determine its effectiveness. As you pick up more schematics, the pool of mods you find in chests or drop from enemies expands, and soon your gun fires corrosive acid, electricity, fire, projectile missiles, and more. Not to mention, mods change how the gun fires, how much damage certain bullets do, recoil, accuracy, and just about any other stat you associate with firing a video game gun. Wild combinations are easy to create, and a unique mod-stacking mechanic that can double or triple effectiveness adds a light touch of puzzle design to this otherwise straight shooter.

Stubby Games smartly emphasizes player expression, never getting in the way of the zanier combinations available to players. The SMG I used to beat the final boss featured mods that made each bullet electric, shot missiles with each shot, covered each bullet in a destructive orb, and featured a ricochet perk that made each bullet bounce off walls and split into even more bullets. I’m thankful for mid-run saves because this SMG permutation, paired with an ability mod that let me throw infinite grenades for a limited time, filled my screen with so much destruction that the entire game crashed. I’d usually bemoan such a thing, but I couldn’t help but laugh. I pushed my PC to its limit with my on-screen chaos.

Boss fights leave a little to be desired – I rarely died because of their simple bullet-hell arenas. Instead, most runs ended because, after bringing down every structure around me, I’d get so lost in the chaos that I wouldn't realize I was stuck in debris while enemies swarmed my location. As stunning as it is to see so much happening on screen, it can be hard to understand what is going on during the most chaotic moments.

Between enemy-filled arenas en route to a stage’s end boss, you might find a shop to buy more mods, ominous obelisks with risk-reward propositions (gain a lot of health or lose half your health, for example), optional trials, and strange phenomena that transport you to different locations. These moments are quick breaks in between bouts of adrenaline-fueled shooter action that I always welcomed – enemies can be relentless, especially as new types are introduced in each stage.

The rest of the Void/Breaker package offers few genre surprises. You can upgrade various traits between runs, research new mod schematics to add to the random pool, purchase new weapons, and discover fun secrets. You can unlock shortcuts, glean in-world information from computer terminals, and hear intriguing dialogue barks from the AI partner who needs your help. It’s all standard stuff for the rogue genre, but if anything, its simplicity pushes you back to the meat and potatoes of this shooter.

Void/Breaker’s shorter runtime – I rolled credits at 12 hours – ensures nothing gets too repetitive in its roguelite structure, but an expansive endgame promises even more to engage with, like different run modifications you can enable to make an already chaotic shooter even more anarchic. I’ll certainly be running it back (again and again) to see what other disruptions I can bring to this AI-simulated adventure. It’s hard not to when destruction feels this good.

Dubbed Traveler on a Winter's Night, Luna 4 introduces three new playable characters, and brings back The Lantern Rite event to celebrate the beginning of the new year.

The first new arrival in Version Luna 4 is Columbina Hyposelenia, the Moon Maiden. Columbina is a 5-Star Hydro Catalyst wielder. Her kit revolves around supporting the squad via Lunar Reactions. She can trigger coordinated Lunar Reaction DMG, even when she’s off the field.

The Moon Maiden’s special ability, Lunar Domain, further boosts all Lunar Reactions by applying a DMG bonus, including summoning more thundercloud strikes for Lunar-Charged reactions. Columbina is also capable of converting Electro-Charged, Bloom, and Hydro Crystallize reactions into Lunar Reactions, as well as revive fallen squad members.

Speaking of elemental reactions, new in this version is Lunar-Crystallize, a new reaction that’s triggered when Geo meets Hydro (under certain conditions). When triggered, Lunar-Crystallize summons three Moondrifts near enemies. When triggered three times, Moondrift Harmony gets activated, dealing Geo DMG to enemies caught in its radius.

Then there’s Zibai, an Adeptus from Liyue. Zibai is another 5-Star character, a Geo Sword wielder. Zibai can, through entering a special state where they can build up energy, unleash an Elemental Skill that deals Lunar-Crystallize DMG.

The longer the fight goes on, the more Lunar-Crystallize reactions are triggered, the higher (and more often) the damage of Zibai’s Elemental Skill becomes.

Luna 4 continues the Nod-Krai story arc, with a big confrontation with Il Dottore. This is the focus of the new Archon Quest, completing which will earn you a new outfit. There’s a gameplay element to that new chapter, too, with the reveal of Piramida, a new area north of the region. Piramida is the headquarters of the Lightkeepers.

The first phase of Luna 4’s Event Wishes will, unsurprisingly, feature Columbina. It’ll also include reruns of Ineffa. The second phase is when Zibai becomes available, alongside another newcomer: Illuga, a 4-Star, polearm-wielding Geo Lightkeeper. The second phase’s rerun will be Neuvillette, who’s also going to have a new outfit in the shop at a discount.

Version Luna 4 brings back the annual Lantern Rite event, taking place in the mainland of Liyue. The event features its own set of minigames with unique rewards, alongside new stories of the Adepti.

All around Liyue Harbor, you’ll be able to place Xiao Lanterns and inscribe them with messages for others to read. You’ll also earn some Fortune Coins from Auspicious Treasure Trees, which you can later exchange for gifts.

All players will receive 1,600 Primogems through the in-game mail. If you log in regularly, you can earn up to ten Intertwined Fates. Lantern Rite has a new outfit for Yaoyao, which is also where you have a chance to earn one 4-Star Liyue character for free.

Finally, you can look forward to the new Classic Mode in Miliastra Wonderland, which lets you invite select Teyvat characters to join you.

#4133. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (2026) Review - Exceptionally Familiar

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo 64 is the most important video game ever made… to me. My byline would not appear in the pages of Game Informer without my original experience playing that game. But it is nearly 30 years old, and despite establishing many important staples of 3D gaming, its age is becoming more apparent. Ocarina of Time was due for a re-examination, and its remake is a wonderful recreation of the 1998 experience with improvements on basically every element: visuals, storytelling, timeless design, and more. It is, however, a remake, and the coloring (though expertly done) is firmly inside the lines.

Ocarina of Time is gorgeous. That the game is less than 25 GB is an engineering marvel. I never quite came around to the odd looks of child Link or Zelda, but every other character, environment, enemy, item, and boss looks incredible. I eagerly looked forward to meeting every weirdo in Hyrule to see their new look, and was never disappointed. The ReDeads and Stalchildren are more traumatic than ever, and every NPC childhood crush I thought I had moved on from was reignited. Watching the sun rise and set over Hyrule feels as magical as it did in the past.

The same accolades can be awarded to the soundtrack. The new orchestrations are incredible, and watching Link’s 4K fingers play the proper notes on his ocarina is mesmerizing. Nintendo continues to fumble voice acting with stiff performances, but thankfully the vast majority of dialogue – one of the primary changes in this remake – is not spoken. Characters don’t necessarily have more to say, but what they say is more impactful, and there are a handful of small but exciting expansions to character and story details. Nothing is groundbreaking or changes how you look at familiar elements, but it manages to be simultaneously nostalgic and improved.

And that’s the closest I got to what I would debatably call a problem: It all looks new, but doesn’t feel particularly new. Ocarina’s overall design holds up. The time travel element is surprising and creates great opportunities to see the world change and evolve; puzzles and their solutions are rewarding; the basics of combat, though simple, are thrilling. All those elements have been adjusted, but not overhauled. Dungeons and their puzzles have been tweaked to remove annoyances (such as fewer keys in the Water Temple), and the new swordplay effects make connecting your blade to monsters feel incredible. But they’re all ultimately small changes that don’t cast Ocarina in a new light or consider its history. It’s a straightforward recreation. But an admittedly very good one.

The biggest, most impactful changes are the new full camera control and active jumping. Swinging the camera around to take a closer look at the upgraded environments is genuinely stirring, especially in the locations that used to be pre-rendered. There is an undefined and exclusive-to-video games emotion I experienced often while trekking locations I thought I knew so well, only to realize I have never seen or looked at it in this way, and I chased and captured that feeling all over Hyrule. Jumping may seem small, but it made me a more active participant in exploration. It also has the benefit of making some encounters feel somewhat trivial (turns out being able to jump over Blade Traps really diminishes their threat), and I was just fine with that.

The beautiful 2026 version of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time does not study the legacy or impact of the landmark game on the video game medium. Instead, it is a meticulous and incredibly impressive recreation of one of the best games ever made. I was rarely surprised during my playthrough, but I was incredibly excited to see old friends and I happily share without embarrassment that playing through its final hour made me cry. For many like me, the original Ocarina of Time is an impactful adventure that arrived at a time in their lives when magic still felt real. Playing the game again 28 years later and appreciating the care taken to maintain and improve that original vision was the ultimate surprise of the whole experience: I didn’t expect to be so moved.

Alex Van Aken contributed to this article.

Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of ar

Certain developers focusing on specific genres is nothing new, especially when they helped define how those genres are perceived in the modern day. While it does wonders to ensure the team is working within their skill set, it can also come back to bite if the genre in question is on the niche side, relying on a smaller fanbase to keep up with constantly rising quality goals.

Arion Kurtaj has pleaded guilty to the 2022 Rockstar Games hack that leaked Grand Theft Auto 6 footage and source code.

In a shocking turn, Firaxis, the team behind massive hits like XCOM and Civilization, has been gutted with the owning company, Take-Two, laying off a whopping third of the studio. With 60 major players ousted, including the head of the studio, the surviving team has been left reeling, still working on long-awaited titles that had yet to turn around.

Firaxis is a very specialized team, working entirely on their series XCOM and Civilization to deliver different kinds of large-scale tactics gameplay to millions across the decades. Now, right after the middling release of Civilization 7 and years into the newest entry in XCOM, losing members is the exact opposite of what the team needs.

Despite this, a spokesperson for Take-Two, Firaxis’ parent company, described it as “restructuring and recentering around the studio’s core strength.” The shrinking team is meant to allow them to operate faster, with a bit of a sleeker ship doctrine to keep things tight as they continue development.

Even so, the team is clearly going to see some major hiccups both in morale and speed, right as the current XCOM project had “...faced development struggles and missed a significant milestone over the summer.” Without major senior staff in the picture, especially the loss of studio head Heather Hazen, I can’t imagine they’ll suddenly be able to hit the ground running.

Firaxis had suffered layoffs as recently as this last September, making this new blow almost feel like a punishment for Civilization 7’s mixed reception. The studio has really struggled to keep up with the constant graphical pushes set by the rest of the industry, with many of their most recent titles suffering from frame issues and performance stutters.

Certain developers focusing on specific genres is nothing new, especially when they helped define how those genres are perceived in the modern day.

Even with their recent hiccups, Firaxis is an absolute titan of strategy gaming, and seeing them continue to spiral is a major blow to the industry. Especially following Take-Two’s major financial win through GTA 6 preorders and the absolute truckload they’re about to make off of the game’s full release, it feels like Firaxis doesn’t need to be hung over the fire like this.

Firaxis is truly one of the original greats, boasting over 30 years of history and genre-defining development that has established what people want from both civilization-building and squad-based tactics. For what it's worth, Firaxis’s mixed launch of Civilization 7 is a major speed bump they needed to be a win.

Their work is some of the most important in the space, bringing tactics titles to millions who wouldn’t have otherwise touched them, giving them an in on a niche but thriving genre that needs the players now more than ever. It feels like the long dev times that have plagued Firaxis have let indie teams and more specialized titles steal their lunch, leaving them out to dry.

It’s hard to say, because performance definitely matters in the gaming industry’s job paths, but this most recent massive cutdown feels shortsighted, to say the least. How is a team that is already struggling to complete a title supposed to speed up after a 33% staff cut, after all? Take-Two has more than enough breathing room, and it feels like they might be getting a little greedy as Grand Theft Auto 6 approaches.

#4131. Heartopia captures the hearts of Animal Crossing and The Sims fans to become the No.1 free download across 50 countries

Heartopia is officially the first big mobile launch of 2026, as the game grabs the attention of millions worldwide.

Heartopia, the new cosy life sim from XD Games, has officially arrived on mobile, right on schedule. If you’ve been keeping up with Heartopia news, you’re likely already aware that the game has pushed back its Steam release to an indeterminate point in 2026.

Doesn’t look like it mattered much, however, as this has already been a big launch on iOS and Android — it probably helps that PC players aren't being entirely left out of the fun, since the game is already available there via XD's own cross-device platform TapTap.

XD Games announced today that Heartopia has reached the top spot on the App Store’s downloads page for free games, and it managed to do so in more than 50 countries and regions worldwide.

The developer is celebratig by offering players a lot of free stuff. If you're feeling lucky, you’ll find new outfits and furniture in three gacha banners (Gilded Acorn Exhibitions): Polar Hymn, The Frostguard, and Coolplayism.

XD Games says you can expect regular updates to add more content, through Fashionwaves and Festivals. In fact, the first season - Winter Frost - is already penciled in for sometime in late January, and it’s going to add appropriately wintery activities like ice skating and snowman-building.

In February, a My Little Pony collaboration event will kick off, bringing new inspired outfits, and vehicles to the game.

Heartopia is a clever mix of Animal Crossing, and The Sims. It’s a free-to-play life sim where you can create your own character, dress them up, build a home for them (and decorate it), and go about town visiting and playing with other players’ characters.

The game’s main feature is the ability to take on a hobby, and seven of those are available at launch. You can dig deep into each hobby, either alone or with others, and there’s a progression track dedicated to each one.

Whether you’re among the millions who downloaded the game already, or you intend to so soon, we’ve got a set of helpful guides to get you started. #4130. Words With Friends picks Whimsy as its first-ever player-selected Word of the Year

I was fully expecting a Gen Z word to win the Words With Friends Word of the Year. I’m technically part of that group myself, and I still couldn’t tell you what half of them mean, but that’s where I assumed things were heading. I was going to work a few of them into the opener to show willingness, but Whimsy isn’t really one for that, so that idea’s gone out the window.

The community vote ran over email and social media, with Whimsy beating runner-up Iconic in the final round. Iconic doesn’t really do anything for me. Whimsy seems like a good pick, though.

In case you’re wondering, Whimsy is basically being playful or fanciful, whether that’s in how someone acts or how something looks. Zynga says it suits a year where people have been going looking for fun in unexpected places.

There’s a Word of the Year tile on the home screen from today, where you can check the pronunciation and definition, and Whimsy is playable in every mode, head-to-head matches and solo puzzles included. It’s six letters with a Y on the end, so it’s a decent way to get rid of high-value tiles too.

Slang did get a look-in last month, though. The dictionary revamp added more than 25,000 new words, modernised definitions and a first-ever way to report words, and slang like Cooked and Lore joined later in the month.

Words With Friends goes back to the Facebook games days, when Scrabble’s own mobile efforts hadn’t really taken off, and Wordle and the other cult-hit word puzzlers have been grabbing the attention for a while now. A vote like this is a nice way to keep people talking about it, I think.

#4129. Diablo 4's long-awaited Tower and its Leaderboards enter beta today, and there's no PTR funny business this time

Diablo 4's first big moment of 2026 is nearly upon us, and it's one feature many have been looking forward to for actual years.

Diablo 4 is about to deliver on Blizzard’s years-old promise to add a challenging, leaderboard-driven experience to the action RPG. The beta for The Tower, and its associated Leaderboards are about to kick off.

As recently revealed, the new experience launches today at 11am PT, 2pm ET, 7pm GMT. This is a beta version that arrives alongside update 2.5.2.

This early launch won’t offer the full experience, and it’s mainly designed to get it into the hands of players early so that Blizzard could get as much feedback as possible and incorporate it into the final version.

The beta is available to everyone, which is a nice change from the usual rigmarole players would have to go through to get the PTR build and play on a different branch. The Tower, and Leaderboards will be available only in the Seasonal Realm, however. Indeed, the plan is to build on what’s there with each future season, so it’s best to think of it as a seasonal experience.

The Tower is about as simple of an activity as you can get in an action RPG. The goal is to climb as many floors as you can as quickly as you can, all while battling increasingly difficult mobs.

You need to reach and beat the Tower’s final boss before you can call it a run. The Leaderboard will then show your time, and let you see how well you did compared to other players.

The Tower is available to anyone who completed Rank 2 of the current Season Rank. Once done, an Obelisk will appear in Cerrigar, letting you access the challenge.

The Leaderboards themselves will operate on a two-week schedule, all of which will take place during a given season. In this case, they’re going to close the day before Season of the Divine Interversion - the game’s current season - ends.

Blizzard published an updated set of patch notes that show how much has changed since The Tower, and Leaderboards first became playable in the patch 2.5.0 PTR.

Though the two new additions have been anticipated for a while, there’s not been much exciting going on in the world of Diablo 4, apart, of course, from the surprise arrival of The Paladin class, which became available in December last year to coincide with the announcement of Lord of Hatred, the game’s next expansion.

#4128. How To Appraise Goods In Probably Stolen

How to inspect goods, evaluate their worth, and level up your appraisal skills in Probably Stolen.

On day eight of running your shop in Probably Stolen, you'll be visited by a member of the Appraisal Board, who has a job offer for you: appraise items for scavengers and get a fee for it. The more you appraise and the better you are at the job, the more you can earn from each appraisal.

So how do you score top dollar in this system? Learn what you're looking at, check your prices, and keep the work consistent. Here's everything you need to know about appraisals in Probably Stolen.

To appraise something is to give an estimate of its value based on its condition, the materials it's made of, and where it comes from. It can also include factors like whether it's a limited edition product or whether it has historical value.

As I said, you unlock appraisals on day eight if you pay the 85 credit fee to join the Appraisal Board. This fee covers your appraisal starter kit: a magnifying glass, a guide for cybernetic hand valuation, and a junior appraisal certificate.

Run the best storefront in the Lower Levels with these Probably Stolen beginner tricks.

For every day that you've got your certificate in your showcase, you'll get at least one customer come to your window with items to appraise. There are three basic categories of items that can be appraised in the game: cybernetic hands, Ribwich sandwiches, and plasma cartridges. They unlock as you rank up your certification.

Accept the Appraisal Board's offer on day eight and pay the 85 credit fee.

The basic appraisal kit and unlocks Cybernetic Hands. 33% chance of an appraisal customer coming in per day.

Get 10 perfect appraisals and pay the 40 credit fee.

Unlocks Ribwiches. 42% chance of an appraisal customer coming in per day.

Get 15 perfect appraisals and pay the 60 credit fee.

Unlocks Plasma Cartridges. 48% chance of an appraisal customer coming in per day.

Get 25 perfect appraisals and pay the 100 credit fee.

55% chance of an appraisal customer coming in per day.

If you don't have the money to pay for your promotion, you can ask the board member to come back in seven days, which gives you a chance to save up. Your certificate stays valid for your current level if you do this, so you can keep appraising in the meantime.

Getting perfect scores on your appraisals is relatively simple. Your guidebooks will tell you exactly what you need to look for, so as long as you follow them carefully, you can get a perfect score every time. Remember, your interactions with customers aren't timed; you can take as long as you need to get everything right. I highly recommend keeping the guidebook open beside your magnifying glass tray. I also recommend going page by page for each item rather than trying to remember the amounts you need to add or subtract.

You're always starting from the base value of the item and adding or subtracting credits based on the characteristics of each one, so any set bonuses are given on top of the base value. You can adjust values at the bottom of the magnifying glass tray in increments of five, 10, and 100 credits in either direction.

#4127. Off the AppStore: Strategic stepping up in Nymble 2

Welcome to Off The AppStore, a weekly feature with a twist. Namely, that while these - as with all the games we cover here - are games that you can play on your phone, they're ones that operate outside of the realms of the big two ways to play: The Google Play Store and the Apple AppStore.

That means that there might be a bit of work required in downloading alternative AppStores or  APKs, or that the games can simply be played in your phone browser. We'll make sure to detail that for each game, though. Anyway, read on to find a new game or experience to play Off The AppStore.

Remember fairytales? Of course you do; they comprise over half of all the inspiration for any given piece of media, and there's nothing wrong with that. There's a reason these stories keep getting told, and that's because of how accessible they are. Even with all the fantastical elements that occur in them, they're still pretty easy to follow and learn from. One such tale is that of Jack and the Beanstalk, which teaches you that it's totally okay to steal as long as you go through a botanically provided backdoor and the target happens to be a giant that would eat you if he could. This is the inspiration for Xalezar, who has given us Nymble 2 (giant presence notwithstanding).

While you're never given a name, you fall into the role of a young and adventurous lad just looking to seek glory and fortune, supposedly. He discovers that he has the unique ability to interact with parts of the world by jumping over them. By using his skill, he has learned that certain patches of land will rapidly grow beanstalks leading to the upper levels of the world, which he will happily climb. It's your responsibility to manoeuvre his jumping effectively so that he can make it to the beanstalk safely.

In order to keep climbing, the boy must keep leaping over fertile beanstalk soil. The challenge is that said patches of land are located in isolated areas that can invite all sorts of danger. Luckily, there are plenty of bountiful treasure chests to find in these lands that the boy can open with his jumping powers. Unfortunately, there are also hostile creatures that will be hunting the boy as he moves around the land. As long as he can get the jump on them, he'll live to make it to the beanstalk and get a few gold stars to boot.

Nymble 2 is the second instalment in the 2D puzzle-adventure series about a boy moving up in the world via jumping and magic plants. It's cute, quick, challenging, and a fun little way to keep your mind active while hanging out wherever you are. The more you climb, the more pieces come into play, and the more you'll have to direct your steps and your jumps. The boy has the power of youthful adventure, but sooner or later, he will have to grow up.

Nymble 2 is available to download and play from its itch.io page!

#4126. Cozy Tanuki Adventure Dev Explains Why It Launched Between Zelda And GTA 6

Most studios wouldn't pick the week between The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time and GTA 6 to launch their debut game, but Denkiworks did. Its cozy adventure, Tanuki: Pon's Summer, arrived on November 10, and the three-person studio says there were good reasons to take the risk.

Discover the official release date and survival mechanics of Wilderdark from the creators of Monstrum.

The Kyoto studio's debut follows Pon, a tanuki delivering packages by BMX while restoring a shrine before a summer festival. It's a very different game from Rockstar's crime epic, but that doesn't make finding an audience in November any easier.

In an interview with GamesIndustry.biz, Denkiworks co-founder and game director Liam Edwards explained why the team stuck with November and what it hopes happens once players have had their fill of the bigger games.

The date wasn't chosen to challenge Nintendo or Rockstar. Denkiworks first aimed for summer but needed longer to finish the game and prepare a multiplatform release. October became the next target, until platform marketing opportunities made November more attractive, Edwards explained.

Less competition doesn't always mean better visibility for a small studio. Denkiworks also secured a publishing deal with Critical Reflex and an early agreement to bring Tanuki: Pon's Summer to Xbox Game Pass. Both offered ways to reach players beyond what the studio could manage alone.

There was another practical hurdle. Denkiworks wanted the game available across PC and consoles at launch, which is a lot to ask of a three-person core team. With help from its publisher, an external porting team handled the Xbox, original Switch, and PlayStation versions, while Denkiworks concentrated on PC and Switch 2. Launching everywhere took coordination, but it also meant players wouldn't have to wait for their preferred platform.

Then came the surprise. Nintendo released its Ocarina of Time remake on November 5, just five days before Tanuki: Pon's Summer. Edwards says the studio couldn't have anticipated the move. That left Tanuki squeezed between Nintendo's game and GTA 6, which launches November 19.

That may be the more awkward overlap. Edwards believes the audience for Pon's laid-back Japanese adventure is more likely to intersect with Zelda players than with people counting down the days to GTA 6. And Ocarina of Time's enormous opening shows just how much attention Nintendo's game has commanded. Trying to compete for the same players in the same week isn't an enviable position for a studio of this size.

Still, it's worth separating the unexpected Zelda release from the studio's own decision. Denkiworks chose November for the opportunities it offered. It didn't knowingly set out to challenge both giants, and Edwards isn't pretending the team can match their marketing budgets.

Rather than trying to win launch week, Edwards hopes Tanuki: Pon's Summer can stick around in people's minds. He described the game as a "lovely little underdog" and suggested that word of mouth could help it find an audience after players have moved on from Zelda and GTA 6. That's a different kind of release strategy from trying to dominate the charts on day one.

Denkiworks is betting that Pon's charm will do some of the work. Alongside delivering mail and performing BMX tricks, players can get to know the island's residents, take part in activities, and rebuild the Great Tanuki Shrine. With so many major releases competing for attention, Pon's laid-back adventure offers something quite different.

For Denkiworks, the goal isn't to beat Zelda or GTA 6. It's to make a game people remember when they're ready to play something else.

For Denkiworks, the goal isn't to beat Zelda or GTA 6. It's to make a game people remember when they're ready to play something else.

That approach isn't risk-free. Launching next to two huge games could bury Tanuki before enough people notice it, and word of mouth isn't guaranteed. But Denkiworks has decided that useful platform support beats waiting endlessly for a perfect date.

#4125. The Sims developer vows "our values are unchanged," as it teases multiple projects from post-Saudi-owned EA

The team behind one of EA's most diverse franchises has issued a statement about its future under the soon-to-be Saudi-owned publisher.

In their (slightly belated) new years message to players, the developer of EA’s The Sims series of games has lightly addressed concerns about its future within the publisher in a wide-ranging letter to the community.

The letter also serves as something of a light plan for what players can expect soon, and in the future, alongside what the various teams are currently working on.

The developer starts off the yearly check-in with a statement that attempts to address concerns about the future of The Sims, historically one of EA’s most inclusive and culturally diverse franchises.

This, of course, comes in the wake of last year’s bombshell that EA is being taken private by a coalition led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), alongside investment firms Silver Lake Capital and Affinity Partners. The $55 billion acquisition was approved by EA’s shareholders in December, and is set to close by the end of June.

Understandably, many raised concerns about what EA’s new ownership would mean for its people, and portfolio of games. The news is concerning for The Sims in particular, a series that’s long embraced diversity and inclusivity, and has historically been popular among women, people of colour, and members of the LGBTQ+ community.

“Our Sims team's creative control, guided by our values of inclusivity, choice, creativity, community, and play, has not changed,” the post reads, though without referring to the buyout directly at any point.

“These values inspire the decisions we make each and every day as we plan for today, tomorrow, and the future.”

As for what’s to come in 2026 and beyond, it sounds like The Sims team has multiple irons in the fire. The developer is working on “a family of new Sims experiences” that will find homes on PC, console, and mobile. Crucially, the post says that not every experience will be on every platform, in order for each to focus on delivering something different and interesting.

Future releases, of course, include new The Sims 4 content that focuses on the single-player experience. The social and more multiplayer-driven experiences, however, will instead be found in Project Rene, the mobile-first life-sim currently in development. (Despite early confidence that it was a working title for The Sims 5, it's now confirmed that Project Rene won’t, in fact, be a direct successor to The Sims 4.)

Some of these projects will see more playtesting throughout 2026, so you should probably sign up for The Sims Labs if you want to hear about when/how you can get involved.

#4121. More Delays Hit MTG Reality Fracture Secret Lair Bundle Right Before Shipping

More shipping woes strike Wizards of the Coast even after all the sets for 2026 have been released.

Delay woes just keep coming for Magic: The Gathering, as fresh delays have hit a recent Secret Lair drop just two days before shipping was due to begin in North America.

In an email sent to some buyers of the Reality Fracture Secret Lair bundle, Wizards of the Coast has confirmed that the planned shipping date of November 19 is now being moved to December 16, almost an entire month after shipping was due to begin.

There are also delays for those in Europe and the UK, which we'll get to, but those orders were already on a later schedule.

The email Wizards of the Coast sent to customers today is, for many, the final straw. Delays and cancellations have been the story of the year in Magic, and it's marred what should have been an otherwise hugely successful year for the game, but the discourse around overprinting products and Wizards biting off more than it can chew has completely dominated the narrative towards the end of the year.

Star Trek stock is still massively delayed for some retailers, meaning pre-orders and back orders still haven't been fulfilled. Total Cards in the UK today reached out to customers to confirm that virtually every product is still delayed in some form.

With the Reality Fracture Secret Lair bundle, however, customers purchased this product under the guise that stock would be sent out relatively quickly, and the planned shipping date of November 19 for North America has been moved to December 16 with 48 hours' notice. The email states that customers can still opt to cancel or amend their orders, but some on Reddit report that payment has already been taken, making it harder to do so.

Elsewhere, the Reality Fracture Secret Lair products were due to ship on December 29 for Europe and the UK, but this has now been shifted to January 19, 2027. This is particularly alarming, as it's just two weeks before the Nauctis: The Sunken Realm prerelease, sparking fears that this latest delay will impact future sets and give 2027 a poor start in terms of availability.

Every set of 2026 has had availability issues in some form, with the problems getting gradually more severe to the point where Star Trek has to cancel the planned beginner box, and some retailers still haven't had their full orders delivered almost two weeks after prerelease.

The lack of transparency around why these issues have been happening is what is stressing players out the most, and while some reasons have been sprinkled in here and there, many announcements are hidden on the Daily MTG feed and are bare-bones statements that confirm the delays rather than explain them. Meanwhile, there's yet another Secret Lair drop happening right now, in addition to last week's Star Trek one.

It really calls into question the business strategy to have so many releases in one year; when you can't meet demand, why wasn't the decision made to slow things down?

Could we see a James Bond Secret Lair, or even a full set, following a teasing Instagram comment after Robert Pattinson's casting confirmation?

Battlefield Studios has released its first official communication in 2026. Rather than unveil the second season of Battlefield 6, however, the developer instead announced a delay. The currently ongoing Season 1 was initially meant to end on Tuesday, January 20, hence why the developer had to communicate something this week.

Season 1 will now end on Tuesday, February 17, which is also when Season 2 will kick off. Given the current sentiment around the game, this news isn’t surprising in the least.

In the blog post announcing the delay, BF Studios said that the decision to extend the current season and push back the start of the next one allows for extra time to “further polish and refine” Season 2 content.

Given that Battlefield 6’s battle royale mode Redsec does not utilise the popular encroaching gas mechanic (using an encroaching ring of fire instead), it’s possible that we may be looking at something new in multiplayer akin to Battlefield 1. Escalating the fight with new threats on the battlefield.Season 2 begins February 17. pic.twitter.com/fGMegJJuTj

What we are getting news of today, however, is the game’s next patch. This extension update is going to arrive next week, on January 20, when Season 1 was supposed to end. You can also expect the free daily login rewards to continue, alongside other periods of double XP.

#4118. Exploring the Science Museum, London for Pikachu in Pokémon Go

Pokemon Go has been hosting tons and tons of collaboration events all throughout the world. There have been tons within the United Kingdom as well, from the National Trust event to their coffee pop-up; these have had varying levels of interaction within the app. So, as the Science Museum in London is so close, we decided to make a trip of it and meet our friends in London to see if we could get some Pikachus!

The Astronaut Pikachu was out globally, but if you catch any in the special gyms at the various science museums that are a part of this collaboration, they have a special location background. I do think that these sorts of backgrounds are so much fun, especially as you can now showcase them on your Avatar Page through your buddy!

When we arrived at the Science Museum in London, we walked through the door and saw a little Pikachu statue, which was stunning! This little detail is a great photo point and the location where you can grab a little bit of paper which tells you about the various Pokemon hidden throughout the museum.

This collaboration felt like a more casual one, similar to the two mentioned above. In-game, there were tons of extra stops and Raids, which provided for a bit of fun. In real life, there were a few different Pokemon banners that had various facts about space. I felt like this is a fantastic way for you to get your young children more interested in space, through the Pokemon connection, but for adults it wasn't a huge, over-the-top, decorated event or anything that felt super Pokemon-esque. It is, still, a very fun collaboration! There are even Pikachu cupcakes in the cafe.

There are some Pokémon-specific items that are for sale in their shop, which you do need a time slot (pre-booked, most of the time) for. These items sell out fast, with a lot of it being kid-aimed, but there are some fantastic Pikachu plushies, sweatshirts, and more that are on offer. It's cute to have a little pop-up shop inside the museum!

We raided a bunch around the museum while checking out the various exhibitions, before stopping at the final point of the museum to get a group picture with the background! If you are interested in the science museum, have a younger kid to take or are just interested in a bunch of Raids, it's a fun partial day out in London.

#4115. Black Mesa’s Latest Update is the Next Best Thing to Half-Life 3

Another year is coming to an end, and (as you and I have gotten used to by now) there’s still no Half-Life 3 in sight. You’d think that 22 years after the release of Half-Life 2, it would hurt any less, but nope.

In a bid to soothe aching hearts and Gordon Freeman enthusiasts all around the world, the wizards over at Crowbar Collective have put out a new update to Black Mesa, making the 2020 love letter to Half-Life look better than ever.

This update, branded a ‘red letter day’ by the developers, focuses first and foremost on visual improvements. Crowbar Collective has managed to make the game look better, while also significantly improving its performance in the process.

After around 20 years at Treyarch, Call of Duty Zombies writer Craig Houston has been laid off, prompting tributes from fans and former colleagues.

In a showcase by the developers, scenes previously clocking around 130 FPS now reach 170 FPS. It’s not clear how these improvements will scale on different hardware, but expect to see noticeable changes across the board.

On the eyecandy side of things, interiors have now been updated to use parallax-corrected cubemaps (PCC). This technique turns static reflections into dynamic ones by adjusting them based on the player’s perspective. As a result, it adds a lot of depth to interiors while not incurring costs on the performance side. Translucent materials like glass have also been updated to have light behave realistically as it passes through.

Another year is coming to an end, and (as you and I have gotten used to by now) there’s still no Half-Life 3 in sight.

While interiors got plenty of jazz, there have also been major improvements to the game’s environmental lighting as a whole. Crowbar Collective has improved the Source Engine’s light bouncing, making indirect illumination behave more realistically. Outdoor scenes have received image-based lighting, using HDR to bring more accurate outputs.

As a love letter to Valve’s magnum opus, it’s only natural for Black Mesa to cater to the company’s handheld console. Following the update’s performance improvements, Black Mesa has received the Steam Deck Verified badge.

The latest update to Black Mesa has modernized the user interface to make it behave better with stick controls, benefiting both Steam Deck and PC users who play with controllers. According to Crowbar Collective, keyboard and mouse have also been refined. Nostalgics can still pick the classic Half-Life menu from the Steam Workshop.

The popular Blue Shift mod by HECU Collective, which tells the game’s story through the eyes of Barney Calhoun, has been updated to be compatible with the latest version of Black Mesa.

For now, this massive update to Black Mesa is all we have until the yearly ritual of hoping for a Half-Life 3 reveal at The Game Awards. Earlier this year, Valve composer Mike Morasky alluded to a certain game codenamed ‘HLX’, which some of the more hopeful types have taken to be a working title for the much anticipated sequel.

That is not the first time Morasky has run his mouth about the HLX project, so maybe, just maybe, this time it’s for real. Until more evidence surfaces, you’ll find me playing Black Mesa.

Black Mesa is available via Windows and Linux platforms via Steam.

#4114. I Wish Had Spoken To Reid Duke Before I Started Playing Magic: The Gathering

We spoke with MTG Hall of Famer Reid Duke about how new players should approach Magic and how it's different now than when he started playing.

Few names are as iconic as Reid Duke in Magic: The Gathering. Picking up the game at just five years old, Reid Duke went on to win the Magic Online World Championship in 2011, six Grand Prix events, and one Pro Tour. Still active in the competitive scene and helping teach the next generation of Magic players, Reid Duke is currently part of team TCGplayer, and when they extended the opportunity to chat with one of the game's legends, it was the fastest I've ever responded to an email.

Fast-forward to our chat, and Reid was exactly as many have already stated: a gentleman. He is easily the nicest person I've ever had the pleasure of interviewing, but better still, he's a fount of knowledge when it comes to Magic, and specifically how new players should approach the game. During our chat, we focused heavily on new players and their progression from discovering the game to picking a preferred format, and everything in between. Here are the highlights from our chat, which includes some advice I desperately wish I'd had when I first discovered Magic over 15 years ago!

The first question I asked Reid was about new players finding their way into Magic. I used my own story as an example: when I first discovered Magic, I had access to cards from a local comic shop, but no LGS to play at, and finding that environment was tough. The only LGS I knew of basically rejected me because I was new, and everyone else was a long-time player who didn't want to teach me. Thankfully, most LGS communities are far more accepting of new players now, and I've always made sure that any store I play at treats all players the same regardless of how long they've played the game. Still, with paper, Online, and MTG Arena as routes into the game, here's what Reid had to say on new players finding their way into Magic:

"I think Arena is a great tool, there are so many ways to engage with Magic, and there's not necessarily a right or a wrong way, but for a new player who doesn't even know how they prefer to engage with Magic, the first thing I would recommend is Arena, because it is so quick, so easy, so accessible. You don't have to put yourself out on a limb in terms of travel, research, or feeling embarrassed to learn the rules of the game in front of experienced players, so there's no beating Arena in terms of accessibility, and it's a really great platform for learning the rules."

Reid would go on to point out the obvious, which is that when he first engaged with Magic, there was no Magic Online or MTG Arena; all he had were the physical cards and the more personal approach of learning the game through making connections with other players, and that route is still extremely valid today, but I completely agree with his point on Arena being far more accessible and, most importantly in the current economy, free.

Four Commander precons for Nauctis: The Sunken Realm have appeared online, and there are some very interesting archetypes in play.

The next question I put to Reid was about Wizards' new-player agenda, and whether it was doing enough to consistently bring new players in and keep them playing. His response was a little unexpected in that, for someone who has been playing for so long, to acknowledge the challenge of getting into Magic due to the core rules is something I figured would be second nature to him now. Here is his full response:

"I think Wizards do a great job of a few things: first, making the best game in the world, but also providing a variety of formats, products and opportunities for players of every level. The biggest obstacle to new player acquisition in Magic is that it's a very challenging game. The rules are hard, and even the most popular casual format, Commander, is very, very complicated, and you encounter a lot of complicated new cards very quickly. New players should be aware that you're going to encounter some challenging stuff as you're learning Magic, but try to be patient and don't get intimidated by that. However, if you manage to get your hands on a beginner box or Foundations kit, you're going to learn the basics a bit quicker, and you can get to the harder mechanics as and when you're ready for them."

I personally didn't consider Magic a complicated game until I started playing games like Lorcana and Riftbound long after I already had Magic pretty much sussed out, but to hear from a 30+ year pro that the game is hard is somewhat validating of those early struggles and should make every player feel better about where they are in their Magic journey.

Now that we've covered some of the routes into Magic and how Wizards is doing at getting new players into the game, I wanted to know where Reid believes new players should go next. Over his career, Reid has played pretty much every format out there at least once (I imagine), but obviously we'd focus on a few core formats as the next step. Here's the advice he has on where new players should look for their first big format commitment:

"Once someone gets their feet underneath them, they've experienced Magic and learned the rules, I would really encourage them to just feel it out and go where the game takes them, and go to the format that's the most fun for them. Now, I will say that my first recommendation for basically anyone is to try Limited. Sealed deck or booster draft, some of the advantages of Limited are that it's a totally even playing field, it's affordable as you don't need a huge collection to get into it, and it's really strong for emphasizing the fundamentals of the game and rules. I think anyone can have fun with Limited, and from there, it's a branching path where, if you have a competitive itch, you will probably go to Standard next, or if your preference leads you to casual Commander, at and LGS or even the kitchen table, that is a super popular way to engage with Magic as well."

This is, and I mean this with zero hyperbole, phenomenal advice. I started playing Limited and prerelease events only in the last few years, and I've become a far better Magic player because of it, but Limited felt intimidating at first. Opening packs and building a deck seemed daunting, but Reid is absolutely right: it's the best and most logical next step once you've grasped the basics.

I genuinely wish someone had given me this advice 15 years ago, because my whole relationship with the game would be completely different, but hopefully, in having this discussion with Reid, there's at least one player out there who will now feel confident enough to just tackle Limited as soon as they're ready, to see where the game takes them next.

When talking a little more about Limited specifically, Reid would expand further on his thoughts surrounding new players engaging with the format.

"Make no mistake, booster draft is played on the Pro Tour at the very highest level, so it's a challenging, deep, engaging format, but I do really strongly believe that it's fun for players at every level, it's a great way to build your collection, learn the rules, and make friends. I would love to highlight prerelease as a really great entry point for players, especially if it's their first time showing up to an LGS and playing with real opponents, because a prerelease is the definition of an even playing field."

As a father actively teaching his daughter to play Magic, I've found the game can be really good for critical and strategic thinking, but it's also a great way to teach reading comprehension and even math. I asked Reid, as someone who started playing at just five years old, whether there is, or should be, a barrier to entry for Magic directly linked to age.

"No barrier to entry. At this point I've taught hundreds of people magic in my lifetime and I have not met someone of any age or background who could not have something to enjoy or learn from Magic."

It's great to hear that Reid is giving back to the game in the form of teaching new players, but even better to hear that he is also of the belief that, if someone wants to learn how to play, there really is no limit that should be applied when it comes to age or background.

I believe there is a ton of value in Magic as a teaching tool. While I've already mentioned that I'm teaching my daughter to play, she has dyslexia, and that can make reading the cards quite tricky, so I try to use the game to aid her reading comprehension and support her already impressive math skills. Granted, this gets much harder when she starts sending an army of goblins to kill me via the Krenko deck she plays with, but that's a small price to pay for the potential upside of engaging her brain with the game.

One final question I had for Reid about new players was around the color pie, and again I pulled from my own experiences with Magic: when I first started playing, I always drifted toward Dimir (black-blue) decks. This was partly because it was the first deck I ever built, the first deck that got me to Mythic on Arena, and the first deck guide I ever wrote on a personal blog.

Over time, I've had to work hard to pull myself away from Dimir decks as a preference in Limited and Standard because it sometimes felt like I was forcing an archetype that wasn't powerful in the moment.

So, I asked Reid whether he has ever struggled with the same issue of color preference, and what his advice would be for new players entering the game.

"Everyone has a preference, one of the great things about Magic is that you can express yourself creatively in deckbuilding and the cards that you choose. My favorite colors are black and green. On the other hand, some of my biggest level up moments as a competitive player and some of my richest experiences in terms of having fun with the game, have been when my friends and teammates have encouraged me to go outside my comfort zone. As a competitive player, you want to go with whatever strategy you believe is best and will give you the chance to achieve your goals, but for anyone at any level, there's no wrong way to do it. Have your preferences, do what's fun for you, just be willing to challenge yourself and go outside of your comfort zone."

It is almost comforting to hear from such an accomplished player that they still need to be pushed outside their comfort zone, and it probably validates the idea that having a preference within the game is completely healthy, provided you're having fun.

Reid was incredible to talk to, and we'll have another part to this interview coming later this week, focusing on the wider game of magic and competitive play.

#4113. After 15 years, The Sims' best spin-off finally gets its due follow-up in The Sims 4: Royalty & Legacy

The Sims Medieval had a short but powerful run back in 2011, and now many of its best features are finally coming to the main franchise.

The Sims 4 developers recently promised an exciting year for the game, and the franchise as a whole, and we just got an early look at one of those first events. After some light teasing, the developer unveiled Royalty & Legacy, the game’s next expansion.

Royalty & Legacy’s first trailer debuted on Thursday, revealing a February 12 release date, and showing off the expansion for the first time.

There’s a lot going on in Royalty & Legacy, which is priced $40. For one, it introduces a new world, Ondarion, which is going to be the setting for your kingdom, as you join a race for the throne. The expansion introduces Dynasty and Nobility - two new systems you can use to create your own world of royal shenanigans.

Ondarion is made up of three neighborhoods (regions). Each region has a unique theme and culture, and they’re each ruled by a Dynasty. Dambele is a place that prioritises art and community. Verdemar is a chaotic world of outlaws and nobles. Finally, Bellacorde is an extravagant region known for opulence and romance.

Speaking of building places, Royalty & Legacy also adds a new Lot type, The Backroom Lot. It serves two functions that change with the time of day. For instance, it can be a library or gym in the morning, and shift into a night club at night. Dambele has its own library-turned-rave, for instance.

At the heart of Ondarion are all the possible fantasy lives and stories you can live. The Sims calls them Powershifts, and they include some well-known Arthurian fantasies and other, more silly ones.

Swordsmanship is the new 10-level skill arriving with the expansion, which further plays into those fantasies by letting your Sims duel. There are even Swordsmanship Tournaments you can watch take place across every neighborhood in Ondarion.

Then there are Secret Passageways, which let you speed up moving across the new regions. They essentially let your Sims teleport between designated passageways, either on their own lots, or other lots in the world. Some of these are hidden for you to find, while others you can create.

In terms of new careers, there’s the Noble Career, where your Sim can rise through several Noble Rankings by doing basically what nobles had to do in the middle ages to earn favour.

The aforementioned Dynasty System is how you can join any of Ondarion’s existing families, or start your own. You actually have a lot of say in what goes on, including the usual business of appointing heirs.

Of course, no royal roleplay would be complete without scandals, which is where the Scandals System comes in. Through it, you can create stories to discredit others, or even topple an entire dynasty.

In November, you may recall The Sims 4 introducing new free items inspired by West African culture. In creating that content, EA worked with a group of Simmers who have direct ties to West African countries.

The group’s guidance was once again utilised to build the Dambele neighborhood in this expansion, and some of the lots around the world of Ondarion were even created by members of the group.

While you wait for Royalty & Legacy to actually arrive, there’s more in The Sims 4 you can jump in right now. The game recently kicked off a collaboration with fashion brand Coach that brought several free items to Create a Sim, and Build Buy. That arrived alongside a free update, which already makes for a busy start of the year for The Sims 4.
